On Wednesday he found the tuner. It was at the bottom of the box, a little clip-on device with a screen, still holding a charge after who knew how many years. He clipped it to the bell, played what he believed was an A, and watched the needle swing and settle. The screen read 440. He frowned at that, played again, held it steady. 440. The A was in tune, apparently, whatever tune meant, and the machine agreed with him.

Then he tried the A an octave up, the way the fingering chart in his method book showed it, and the screen jumped. Not to 445, not to 450. To 880. He sat very still on the edge of his bed with the horn warm in his hands. He played the low A. 440. The high A. 880. Exactly double, both times, and a third time, and a fourth, the digits landing clean with no wobble in between.

"Deej," he said into his phone, "what's A440 mean?"

"It means A, man. Concert pitch. Why."

"The tuner says 440 on the low A and 880 on the high one. Same note, one octave up. Double."

"Show me tomorrow."

Deej came over Thursday after cross-country practice, still in his spikes, and stood in James's room with the door shut because James's father had made it clear that the household had opinions about the trumpet after ten p.m. Deej played low A, watched the screen, played high A, watched it double, and said, "One octave higher vibrates at exactly twice the frequency. So that A above A440 is 880 hertz. That's what the screen's telling you."

"So it's not broken."

"It's the opposite of broken." Deej tapped the tuner with one muddy finger. "It's math."

James stared at the two numbers, 440 and 880, the way you stare at something that has been true your whole life without your permission. Everything he'd practiced on the clarinet, every scale, every etude, had been sitting on top of this the whole time, numbers underneath the notes like bones under skin. He didn't feel smarter. He felt late.

Friday night his father knocked once and came in without waiting. James lowered the horn. On the desk between them, the tuner's screen still glowed with the last note, an A held too sharp, the needle leaning right like a compass near a magnet.

"You sound better," his father said. Not kindly, not unkindly. Factually.

"It's math," James said. "The whole thing. I thought it was, I don't know, magic."

His father picked up the tuner, turned it over in his hands, and set it back down. "Your grandfather used to say you could tune a whole band off one note. I thought he was showing off." He stood there a moment longer, then said, "What time's this audition?"

"Ten in the morning. I still can't play the high part. The C above the staff. It comes out like a scream."

"Play it," his father said, and sat down on the bed.

James raised the horn. The tuner's needle woke and swung left, searching, and he pressed his lips together and thought about the number the C might be hiding underneath it, whatever doubling and doubling had built it, and blew.

Christian kept the sample ballot folded in his back pocket all through fourth period, and by the time he sat down in Mr. Reyes's government class, the paper had gone soft at the crease. The room still smelled like the floor wax the custodian had laid down over the weekend, and the radiator under the window ticked in its own private meter. On the whiteboard, in Mr. Reyes's looping hand, was written: Election Day. Polls close at 7:00. Nobody checks whether you went.

Dara leaned across the aisle before the bell finished. "Are you voting after school or before?" she asked. "Because I have practice at four, and my mom said she'd drive us at five, but only if we're back by six."
"After," Christian said. "I have to eat first. My grandmother's making dinner early because of it." He said this as though it explained something, and in his family it did. His grandmother had announced on Sunday that she intended to feed him properly before his first vote, the way you might feed a boxer.
"You know," said Marcus from the row behind, "my brother didn't vote until he was twenty-three. Said it didn't matter." Marcus was seventeen and jaundiced about nearly everything, in the general way of seventeen-year-olds who have recently discovered that adults improvise.
"It matters to my grandmother," Christian said. At Sunday dinner she had told the story, unprompted, fork suspended over the potatoes. She had turned eighteen in 1970, she said, married already, working at the phone company, and she had not been allowed to vote. Not at eighteen. The law changing that, the amendment, was ratified in 1971, and it had taken about three months, faster than any other amendment to the Constitution. Christian had stopped chewing. Three months felt impossible. His mind kept trying to transmute the fact into something he recognized, some equivalent, and failing. He had said, "Wait, so people your age, they just, couldn't?" and his grandmother had laughed and said, "We could be drafted, honey. We just couldn't vote on anything," and his grandfather had put down his glass and left the table for a minute, which nobody commented on.

Mr. Reyes started class by asking who had registered, and eleven hands went up, which was more than Christian expected. "Good," Mr. Reyes said. "Now. Today's not a pep rally. I want you to look at the sample ballot and find one race you know nothing about. Raise your hand when you find it." Every hand went up again, slower this time. Christian's blank race was for a county water board, an office so obscure it sounded like something from a novel. "That's the honest part," Mr. Reyes said. "Not knowing. The dishonest part is pretending you know."
Christian copied the water board candidates' names onto a scrap of paper. He had been planning to skip that race entirely, to vote only where he had opinions, but something about the exercise annoyed him pleasantly, the way a pebble in a shoe makes you notice your own walking. Dara nudged him. "I'm asking my dad about the water one," she whispered. "He complains about our water pressure like it's a moral issue."

The class argued about whether a single vote mattered, and Marcus made his case with statistics he half-remembered, and a girl named Priya said that the argument itself was the point, that the vote was a kind of speech, and Christian found himself thinking about three months. About a whole country deciding, in a season, that eighteen-year-olds were citizens in the fullest sense. He had always assumed eighteen was simply when voting began, the way eighteen was when a lot of things began, a fact with no history, like gravity. It had a history. It had a grandmother at a table with a fork in the air.
"I read that the amendment setting the voting age at eighteen went through in about three months," he said, out loud, surprising himself. "In 1971. It was the fastest one ever ratified."
"Correct," Mr. Reyes said, and moved on to polling locations, because Mr. Reyes never gave speeches about anything, which was either modesty or strategy.

At five fifteen, Dara's mother's car smelled like hair spray and fast food, and the line at the elementary school gymnasium curved past the folding tables and out under a banner the PTA had made. Christian checked his watch too often. Dara's practice had been sacrificed; her coach had said "family thing?" and she had said "democracy thing," and that had been allowed. An older woman ahead of them in line dropped her pen and Christian picked it up, and she said, "First time?" in a way that suggested his face had already answered.
"How can you tell?"
"Everyone checks the machine like it's going to disagree with them." She smiled. "My husband was twenty when that amendment passed. He voted that same year. Talked about it until he died."

When Christian's turn came, the machine took his selections with small clicking sounds, each one a little louder in his ears than it could possibly have been. He voted for the things he knew. He came to the water board, the two unfamiliar names on his scrap of paper, and held his finger over them both. Dara was two machines away, frowning at her ballot with the concentration of someone defusing something. The clock above the gym door said 6:41.

He looked at the names a moment longer. Then he made his choice, and the machine clicked, and he stood there in the November light of the gymnasium wondering whether his grandmother, at her table right now with the good plates out, had ever once, in fifty years of voting, felt certain she was right.

The bus smelled of diesel and grape juice, and Gabrielle had claimed the back seat with her knees up and the paperback open flat against them, running a pencil down the margin of chapter one. She had started the novel at seven that morning, finished it at lunch, and felt personally betrayed by page two hundred and something, and now she was going back to find every place the lying had started.

"You're rereading it already?" Dana dropped into the seat across the aisle, ponytail swinging. "It's been out since before my mom was born. It's called The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. Agatha Christie, 1926. You thought the butler did it?"

"Don't say anything else," Gabrielle said, holding up the pencil like a tiny fencing foil. "You already ruined my life once today."

"I told you the narrator did it. That's not ruining, that's education." Dana leaned over and tapped the cover, where a dignified doctor's face loomed. "Dr Sheppard. He narrates the whole book, and he's the murderer. The whole time. That's the trick."

Gabrielle had not believed her at first, because Dana's track record on spoilers included a French film she had described entirely wrong and an incident with a cake recipe. But the book club met Thursday, and the book club had chosen this novel specifically because Mrs. Okafor's list called it "the great experiment in unreliable narration," and Gabrielle wanted to walk in with evidence instead of outrage. So she reread, and the rereading was strange. Every sentence had two faces now. When Dr Sheppard wrote that he had a few things to dispose of, she had read it as a man tidying his papers; now it sat on the page like a wink she had missed. She flagged it. She flagged the paragraph where he described leaving the study and locked the gate behind him, unhurried, precise, a man with all the time in the world because he had made the time himself.

The bus jolted over the crossing on Miller Road and her pencil skidded a grey comet across the page. Behind her, Theo was narrating his own unreliable account of the basketball game to a row of freshmen, embellishing with every retelling. "And then I dunked it," he was saying, though Gabrielle had watched him miss twice.

"You fell," she called back over the seat. "I was there. You fell on Marcus."

"The narrator has a perspective," Theo said with dignity, and the freshmen laughed, and Gabrielle laughed too, because it was a joke, and also because it was exactly her homework.

By the time the bus turned onto the hill road she had nine flags, and she had begun to notice something odd, which was that Dr Sheppard never actually lied. He said he would not write certain things down. He said the reader would learn everything in due course. He was slippery the way a kid is slippery when you ask who broke the lamp, technically accurate, carefully incomplete. It reminded her of her own college application essay, three drafts of which had been truthful and none of which had been honest, and she had eventually shown the real one to her mother, which had gone better than expected, a small rapprochement achieved over the kitchen table and a plate of shortbread.

Dana migrated back a row and read over her shoulder, chin hooked on the seat. "Ooh, you found the gate bit. That's the famous one. Mr Kavliek talks about it every year, very incisive, he does a whole bit with a transparency."

"I want to find it myself first," Gabrielle said. "Before anyone explains it to me. Because the thing I keep wondering is whether I could have caught him, or whether the book doesn't let you. Whether it's a fair puzzle or just a trick."

"Maybe both," Dana said. "Maybe that's the point, that you trusted him for two hundred pages for no reason except that he was talking."

"Trust doesn't atrophy that fast," Gabrielle said, and then considered it. "Actually, maybe it does. One betrayal and I'm out here flagging commas."

The bus lurched to its stop and the aisle filled with backpacks and shoving. Gabrielle closed the book with the pencil still inside it, like a bookmark holding a case file shut. Thursday was two days away. She had the gate, the disposal line, the too-calm walk home, and a suspicion, still unproven, about the typewriter. She could be wrong about the typewriter. She had been wrong before, spectacularly, about the butler.

"Coming?" Dana said from the steps.

"In a second." Gabrielle stood in the emptying bus, thumb on the pencil, looking at the cover, where the doctor's face still looked trustworthy, in the way that faces do. She opened the book again to page nine and started walking down the aisle, reading, one hand trailing along the seat backs.

Riley found the recipe at eleven in the morning, folded into the back of his mother's cookbook like a letter someone had started and never mailed. Chicken with lemon and herbs, for four. His parents were due home at six from the hospital where his grandmother had been since Tuesday, and his brother Marcus had texted from college that he was driving up, which meant dinner had to be real, not pasta from a box. Riley wanted to make the kitchen into a place people wanted to enter tonight, and he wanted to do it himself, without calling his mother to ask her anything.

He read the recipe through once, then again. Chopped parsley, lemon zest, garlic minced fine, a whole cut-up chicken, olive oil, butter, an egg for brushing the crust of the bread he'd decided to add because bread felt like an event. He liked the logic of a recipe, the way each sentence assumed the next one. He set the chicken in the sink to thaw the rest of the way and started chopping, and the kitchen began to smell like parsley and raw garlic, which was the smell, he thought, of something about to become dinner rather than the smell of dinner itself.

His phone buzzed on the counter. Marcus: "Is gran ok?" Riley typed "stable" and then deleted it and typed "we'll know more by tonight" and set the phone face down. He crushed the garlic instead, with the flat of the knife, because he'd seen a video once and wanted to know if it worked. It did. The clove split open under the blade like something unclasping, and he stood there a second, wondering how many things worked like that, how many things only needed to be pressed in the right place.

He browned the chicken in butter. That part went well, better than he'd expected, the skin going the color of an old photograph, and he moved the pieces to a plate and built the sauce in the same pan, scraping up the browned bits with broth while the juice of a whole lemon went in. Then he turned to the bread, softened the yeast in warm water, stirred in flour and salt, and reached into the refrigerator for the egg to brush on top before baking.

There were no eggs. Not one. The carton sat on the shelf with its lid open and nothing inside, and Riley stood holding it like a man reviewing his own solvency and finding the accounts empty. Marcus had made omelets on Sunday, apparently, all of them, and had said nothing, and Riley privately excoriated him for it, then felt the criticism dissolve, because would he himself have mentioned it? He would not have. He checked the bowl of dough rising under a towel on the counter, then the clock, then the recipe, where the egg was listed in the second line, in the ingredients, where he had not read carefully because he'd been reading for feeling the first time and for method the second.

The store was a fifteen-minute round trip if he ran. He could go, or he could skip the wash and bake the loaf plain, or he could start over on the bread entirely, and none of those felt like nothing. While he stood deciding, he thought about the cooking videos again, how the cooks always had every ingredient in little glass bowls before they started, chopped and measured and lined up, and he'd assumed that was for the camera, for show. Now he wondered if it was the whole point. If he had set out the egg this morning, an empty carton would have told him something at ten o'clock instead of at noon. He looked up the phrase on his phone with butter still on his thumb. Mise en place. It meant putting in place, measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.

He ran to the store. On the way back, cutting through the park, he passed the small stone outcrop where his father had once shown him a sign about montane habitat, the kind of high, cold ground certain plants and birds needed, and Riley had asked whether the park could really count as montane and his father had said that depended on who drew the lines. He thought about that now with the eggs cold against his palm. His grandmother's doctors kept drawing lines too, saying she was stable and she was responding and she was not out of anything, and each word seemed to mean both more and less than it said.

He brushed the loaf with egg, sprinkled it with salt, and slid it into the oven. Then, because there was time, he took out every remaining ingredient for the rest of the meal and put them in bowls on the counter in a row: the chicken on its plate, the sauce waiting in the pan, the lemons, the parsley already chopped, the butter, the salt. It looked almost ridiculous, a dinner laid out like a still life, and he liked it anyway. Maybe the French cooks had it right and maybe it was just a way of pretending you could know the future, and Riley stood there unable to decide which it was, and not sure the two were even different.

The headlights came up the driveway at six-twenty, both cars, and Marcus's behind them. Riley took the bread out, set it on the rack to stop cooking, and heard the front door and his mother's voice saying something low to his father that he couldn't make out, which meant either very good news or very bad, and he would know in a moment and there was no bowl for that, no way to measure it out in advance. Marcus came into the kitchen first, dropped his bag, and stared at the row of little bowls on the counter.

"What is all this," Marcus said.

"Everything we need," Riley said, and wiped his hands on the towel, and went to find out about their grandmother.

Elizabeth had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at three o'clock, and by five she had filled six pages of a legal pad with crossed-out sentences. Her paper was due in eleven days, and Mr. Okafor had rejected her first attempt with a single line of red pen: "This is a report. I asked for an argument."

The public library smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue. Outside, October was dismantling the maples along Bergen Street, and through the tall windows she could watch the leaves come down while she avoided the page. Her topic was the juvenile court system, whether sixteen-year-olds should be tried as adults for violent crimes, and she had chosen it because her cousin DeShaun had been tried as an adult at sixteen, in a courtroom Elizabeth had not been allowed to enter. She had been thirteen. Her mother had said, stay home, and she had stayed home, and she had never decided whether staying was loyalty or cowardice.

The problem was that she had facts but no position, or rather two positions, and each one wanted the whole page to itself. When she wrote from DeShaun's side, the sentences turned into a sermon, all heat and no hinges. When she wrote from the other side, the side her uncle the prosecutor would have taken, the prose went cold and evasive, hiding behind words like "accountability" without saying what they cost. She needed a way to hold both, and she did not know one.

At the next table, a boy from her AP US History class, Tomas, was slamming a style guide shut with theatrical despair. "Footnotes," he said to no one in particular. "Whoever invented these rules should be tried for crimes against students."

The reference librarian, a small woman named Ms. Prieto who wore her badge crooked, looked up from the returns cart. "The Chicago Manual of Style," she said. "Its notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes. It was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906."

Tomas stared. "Nineteen oh six?"

"That's older than my great-grandparents," he said, and seemed to find this genuinely troubling, as if the rules had acquired seniority, the right to be obeyed simply by outliving everyone who might have complained.

Elizabeth copied the call number from the spine when he set it down. She carried the Manual to her table and opened it, expecting bureaucracy, and found instead a kind of architecture. The footnotes were not decoration; they were a second argument running beneath the first, a quiet ledger of debts. Each note said: I learned this here, from this person, on this page, and you may go check. She thought of Mr. Okafor's red line, and of her uncle, and of DeShaun, and understood suddenly that an argument was not a fist. It was a claim standing on the record of what it owed.

She worked until the overhead lights clicked to their evening half. First she drafted a thesis she could actually defend: that transfer to adult court, whatever its logic for violent offenses, should require a judge's individual finding rather than automatic prosecution by statute, because DeShaun's case had turned on a mandatory statute and a judge who said, on the record, that his hands were tied. Then the footnotes, numbered, each one a small confession of source. When she reached for the case citation she found she could not remember whether the statute came from 2016 or 2018, and she wrote both possibilities on the pad and left a note to herself: check. The uncertainty did not feel like failure. It felt like honesty with a number attached.

She tried to explain this to Tomas on the way out, proselytizing a little, she admitted, the way anyone does after a conversion. "It's like the syntax of trust," she said. "Where the note goes, and what comes first, and what you admit you don't know. It's not sectarian, it's not one side's ritual. It belongs to whoever uses it honestly."

"You're describing paperwork," Tomas said, holding the door.

But walking home under the stripped maples, carrying the bag with eleven days of work in it, Elizabeth kept thinking about the ledger underneath, about 1906, about all the dead people who had argued in notes and been checked and been right or been corrected. And she thought again of the afternoon she stayed home, thirteen years old, obedient, sure that following a rule was the same as supporting a person. At the corner of Bergen and Sixth she stopped, took out her phone, and dialed the number for the county records office, the one she had found in the library's database but been afraid to use.

"Records division," a voice said. "We closed at five."

"Tomorrow, then," Elizabeth said, and put the phone away, and the manual, checked out in her name, sat in the bag on her hip, already three days overdue.

Sophia's grandmother had always bought her tomatoes from the third stall on the left, the one with the crooked hand-painted sign, and so Sophia went there first, even though the tomatoes at the entrance looked just as good and were fifty cents cheaper a basket. The market had been going since seven and by ten the asphalt was giving back heat in slow waves. She held the list her mother had texted against the wind and worked down it: tomatoes, bread, a wedge of cheese, eggs from the Hsu farm if they still had any.

She was making dinner tonight, the whole thing, because her parents had driven to her aunt's to help move furniture and wouldn't be back until late, and because her brother Danny had asked her to, which he never did. He was leaving for basic training in three weeks and had requested one specific meal, their grandmother's pasta with fresh tomatoes and the slow-scrambled eggs she used to fold in at the end. Sophia had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to, which was a kind of cooking that depended on a woman who had died in March.

The Hsus had eggs. She bought two dozen, more than she needed, because their carton was cold to the touch and it made her feel competent to plan ahead. Then she stood too long at a table of honey and jam, texting a friend about dorm assignments, and then longer still arguing pleasantly with the cheese man about whether pecorino or the cheaper local sheep's cheese was closer to what an Abruzzese grandmother would use. He gave her a taste of both. She bought the local one, then walked three stalls and turned around and bought a small piece of the pecorino too, because she could not decide, and because undecided felt, this summer, like its own small malaise she couldn't name.

It was past noon when she got home. She put the bags on the counter and stood in the kitchen with the door open behind her, letting the screen door bang the way her grandmother used to when her hands were full. The eggs sat in their bag. The cheese sat in its paper. The tomatoes, at least, she set out on the windowsill, because that was what her grandmother did, and the image of them there, fat and red against the glass, steadied her.

She cooked for two hours. The sauce took longer than the recipe card said, because the recipe card assumed you already knew things, assumed you knew that the garlic should barely color and that the tomatoes would give up their water if you just refused to hurry them. The eggs she scrambled on the lowest flame, stirring in figure eights, and when she folded them into the finished pasta the whole kitchen smelled like being eleven years old. Danny ate two plates and kept saying the word exactly, as in, this is exactly it, and their younger sister Lucy ate one plate and then asked if she could take the rest to her friend's house tomorrow because her friend's mother worked nights and never cooked.

So there were leftovers, a big steel bowl of them, and it was Lucy's question that made Sophia look at the clock. Four hours, she realized, since she'd left the market with the eggs, and the eggs had spent that time in a bag, then in the car, then on the counter while she cooked. She'd read something once, in the food safety unit of a class she'd half slept through, and now she dug through her phone to find it. Perishable food shouldn't sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours. She read it twice. And one hour, the page said, if it's above 90 degrees out. She checked the weather app. Ninety-four.

"Where are the eggs?" she asked, and her voice came out sharper than she meant.

Danny, nonchalant, feet up on a chair, pointed at the counter. "Right there. Why?"

Sophia stood very still, holding the phone, doing the arithmetic. The eggs had been out at least four hours in a kitchen that had to be eighty-five, maybe more, with the oven running. The cooked pasta was newer, but it had been sitting out while they ate, and it was nowhere near the fridge. She thought of her grandmother, who left things out all day and waved off worry, and of her mother, who refrigerated butter. Two people she loved, two completely opposite instincts, and neither of them had ever stated a rule. She was tired of inheriting positions without reasons.

"The eggs are done," she said. "I can't use them. They've been in the danger zone way too long. The pasta I can save if I move it now, it's only been out about an hour, but the raw eggs are out." She heard herself and worried she sounded like a pamphlet, but Lucy was already looking at the bowl with narrowed eyes.

"So we can't give any to Kayla tomorrow?"

"We can give her the pasta. If it goes in the fridge right now." Sophia carried the bowl to the refrigerator, and the cold air on her wrists felt like arriving somewhere. She came back and scraped the eggs into the trash, all two dozen, the carton that had felt so reassuringly cold at eight in the morning. It was only money, she told herself, and then stopped telling herself things, because the loss was real and pretending otherwise was its own kind of dishonesty.

"You could've asked me," Danny said. "I know that stuff. We get it drilled into us. Two hours, one if it's hot out, above 90." He said it without any accusation, just handing her the fact the way you'd hand someone a tool they were already reaching for.

"You could've mentioned it four hours ago," she said, and he laughed, and she laughed, and then she went back to the recipe card and turned it over and wrote on the back, in her grandmother's old pencil stub, what she had learned, so that next time the knowledge would be in the family and not just in her phone. At the bottom she added the shopping order for a second attempt at the eggs, and under it a note to buy a cooler for the drive home from the market.

Then she texted her mother: pasta safe, eggs a loss, will contextualize later. And after a minute she picked up the pencil again and crossed that out and wrote, more simply, it's a long story, I'll tell you when you're home. She put the tomatoes back on the windowsill, the ones she hadn't cooked, and set one in the center of the sill where the light would find it in the morning.

The seminar room on the third floor of Hollis Hall had one window that faced the parking lot, which struck Jeremy as either poor planning or an accident of prophecy. Twelve students sat around a table with the professor, who had assigned them a city council transcript from a town called Fenwick, where the council had spent four hours arguing about whether to raise the downtown parking fee from two dollars to three. Jeremy had read it twice on the bus, twice more at his desk, and had underlined so many passages that the underlining had stopped meaning anything.

"Who wants to open," Dr. Okonkwo said, not quite making it a question.

Priya opened. She had prepared, which was her way of saying she had prepared. "The fee is too low," she said. "Three dollars still wouldn't cover the maintenance, and the overflow parking spills into the Elm Street neighborhood, so residents can't park in front of their own houses. The fee should be five."

Marcus countered that five dollars would push commuters to the mall on the highway, which would kill the downtown businesses, which would shrink the tax base, which would, he implied, eventually cause the heat death of Fenwick. A girl whose name Jeremy kept forgetting argued for a sliding scale by income. Someone else proposed validation stickers for local shops. The debate had the shape of an archipelago: eleven separate islands of argument, a thin channel of civility between each, no bridge anywhere.

Jeremy had not prepared a position. What he had was a memory, from the night before, of his roommate Dev scrolling past a meme and saying, "Oh, that's the Meadows thing," and refusing to elaborate because his show was starting. Jeremy had typed the name into the library database at midnight and found a 1997 essay about leverage points. He had read it in the common room under a diaphanous curtain of moths swarming the porch light, and certain sentences had rearranged the furniture in his head without asking.

He raised his hand, mostly to stop Priya from parametrizing the fee schedule any further. "Can I ask whether we're solving the right thing?"

"That's not a real objection," Priya said. "Everything is the right thing if you care about it."

"Sure. But the council spent four hours on the fee. Nobody asked why the city is organized so everyone drives downtown alone and leaves at five." He was aware his voice had gone up, and lowered it. "There's this essay. Donella Meadows, 1997, on leverage points. She argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much. Changing a system's goals, or the paradigm underneath it, changes the most."

Dr. Okonkwo's eyebrows did something small and interested, which Jeremy chose to read as encouragement.

"So the fee is a number," he went on. "We could fight about two dollars or three or five forever, and Meadows would say we're turning a dial that barely moves anything. If Fenwick actually wanted fewer cars downtown, the goal would have to change. Or the paradigm. The whole picture of what the street is for."

Marcus leaned back. "That's convenient. Your essay says the thing you want to argue can't be costed out."

"It's not my essay."

"It's also unfalsifiable," the girl whose name was, Jeremy now remembered, Talia, said pleasantly. "You can't run the experiment twice."

This was, Jeremy had to admit, true, and he said so, which in his experience of seminars was a tactical error, because admitting things invited more of them. Priya asked whether a paradigm was just a word people used when they didn't want to do math. Dr. Okonkwo asked whether Meadows herself had said anything about how paradigms get changed, and Jeremy had to say he'd gotten to the last section at two in the morning and remembered only the part about paradigms changing all the time anyway, in societies, without anyone planning it, which was either hopeful or terrifying depending on the century.

The problem, as Jeremy framed it for himself on the walk back across the quad, was that he believed two things at once. He believed Meadows, that the fee debate was a hall of small mirrors, and he believed Priya, that the residents of Elm Street needed relief this year and the fee was the lever actually attached to the machine. He had spent the seminar trying to get the two ideas to sit in the same chair, and they had refused, and he had ended by proposing, out loud, almost by accident, that Fenwick raise the fee to three and put the revenue toward a downtown where the fee itself could eventually shrink, which Marcus called incoherent and Talia called the only honest position anyone had taken all morning and Priya called a cop-out. He did not know which of them was right. He suspected that not knowing was, for the moment, the most accurate thing he had.

The parking lot below the seminar window had been nearly empty all morning, and Jeremy noticed, as they filed out, that it was nearly full. Somewhere a bell rang the hour. He stopped at the railing, took out his phone, and, instead of opening anything, just photographed the lot, rows of cars baking in the October sun.

"For the paradigm," Talia said, passing behind him.

He looked at the photo. "I was going to say for the fee."

"Same picture," she said, and walked on toward the science building, leaving him holding the rail and the phone and, for once, both of them.

The rental truck followed them the whole way, and Morgan kept checking the side mirror to make sure it was still Dad behind the wheel and not some stranger hauling her boxes to a town she had agreed to only twice out loud. In the passenger seat, her grandmother sat with a road atlas open on her knees even though the phone was navigating, because she liked to know where she was in a way the phone never told her.

"You could have flown ahead with your mother," her grandmother said. "This is forty hours of road for a girl your age."

"I wanted to drive." Morgan had her own reason, though she had not said it in the car. Priya and Denae were meeting her at the pancake place on Route 9 at noon, one last breakfast before the truck got too far east to turn around. That was the plan. The plan had a hole in it, which was that after the pancakes there was nothing but four hundred more miles.

Grandma Ruth had her own want, and it had to do with the boxes in the truck. She was moving into the new house with them, giving up the apartment she had kept alone for nineteen years, and twice this morning she had asked whether the movers had wrapped her writing desk. She wanted, Morgan understood, to be the one who decided what got brought and what got left, and she was doing it by making lists on the back of a grocery receipt.

They stopped at the pancake place for fifty minutes. Priya was late and Denae was early and they split a short stack three ways, and Denae made a joke about Morgan's new town that started funny and turned vitriolic halfway through, about the people there, the kind of people who would love her, the kind who had never met her. Morgan laughed at the first half and then stopped laughing and said, "You don't know them either." Nobody said anything for a while after that. Priya took a photo of the three of them at the table, and it came out blurry, and she said she'd take another one, and then didn't.

The night before, they had all sat on Denae's garage roof, the way they had since seventh grade, and Priya had said the thing Morgan was now thinking about in the car. "It's not like we'll be strangers," Priya had said. "We'll text every day." And Denae had said, "No, we won't, we'll mean to," and it had sounded harsh but Morgan had known it was the more honest sentence. Friendship, she was beginning to see, was not only a feeling. It was a set of conditions, some of which nobody chose.

She had learned the actual evidence for that in June, killing time in the library while her mother packed dishes. She had been reading about college, about how to make friends in a place where nobody knew her, and she found a study from 1950 by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, and Kurt Back, done in student housing. The students had all been assigned their rooms more or less at random, which was what made it a study rather than an accident. The researchers found that people living closer together were more likely to become friends. People whose doors were near a shared stairway became friends more often too, because the stairway made them pass each other. Morgan read it twice. It wasn't shallow, she decided, or if it was, it was the shallow part of something real. You could love someone and never see them, and the love would sit there like a letter nobody opened.

"There's a stairwell apartment," Grandma Ruth said around dinnertime, somewhere in Ohio. "In the new house. Your father gave me the room by the back stairs."

"That's the Festinger room," Morgan said.

Grandma Ruth looked over. "The what?"

"Nothing. A study. People near the stairs make more friends. From 1950. Festinger, Schachter, and somebody named Back." She paused. "You'll be the popular one."

"I was planning on it," her grandmother said, and made a note on the grocery receipt.

Morgan texted Priya from a gas station outside Zanesville: ask Denae if she's still mad. Priya wrote back that Denae wasn't mad, she was just Denae, and then sent the blurry photo after all. Morgan looked at it under the fluorescent awning, three faces smeared by motion, and set it as her lock screen anyway. She did not know yet whether the study meant she should stop grieving the old friends or start forgiving the new ones in advance, or whether it meant nothing a person could act on at all. Probably, she thought, she would find out in September, and probably by accident, the way the students in the housing had. The truck's headlights swung into the lot behind them, and her father got out stretching his arms, holding the keys up so she could see them glint under the lights.

Colton arrived at fifth period with the essay prompt already folded into his back pocket, though he had written nothing but a single underlined sentence: Who do you trust in Wuthering Heights, and why? He had read the whole novel in nine days, mostly on the bus, and somewhere around chapter nine he had begun to feel that the story kept catching in a filter, the way pond water looks different through a dirty jar.

Ms. Reyes had pushed the desks into a circle, which Colton hated, because circles demanded speech. She asked who narrated the book, and Drew Oliphant said Catherine, which was wrong, and then Priya said Heathcliff, which was also wrong, and then the room went quiet in the way rooms do when everyone is waiting for someone else to be wrong in a more interesting fashion.

"It's the housekeeper," Colton said, surprising himself. "Nelly Dean. Most of the book is her telling the story to this visitor, Lockwood. He's renting a house from Heathcliff, he gets sick, and while he's stuck there she tells him everything. So it's not like a normal narrator. Everything gets to us through both of them."

Priya leaned forward. "But wait. Didn't Nelly hate some of those people? Does that change how she tells it?" She had a pencil behind her ear and a paperback bristling with pink tabs. "Like, when she describes Catherine, is she describing Catherine or describing her own grudge?"

Colton opened his book to a page he had dog-eared without admitting it to himself. He had marked the spot where Nelly admits she warned Heathcliff about Hindley's plan to separate him from Catherine, an intervention that had consequences Nelly then narrated as though she had merely been a bystander. "She says she was only giving information," he said slowly, "but she chose which information. She's in the story and telling the story at the same time."

"That's an unreliable narrator," Priya said.

The phrase landed in Colton strangely, because he recognized the shape of it from somewhere outside the classroom. Last spring he had sat in his grandfather's kitchen while the old man explained, overCards and coffee, why Colton's mother didn't speak to her brother, and Colton had listened and believed every word, and only later, at Thanksgiving, heard his uncle's version of the same year, which matched his grandfather's in dates and almost nothing else. Neither man had lied, he thought now. Each had simply been the housekeeper of his own account, arranging the furniture of the past so that he stood in the most defensible corner of the room.

He said none of this aloud, but the inchoate idea pressed at him for the rest of the discussion. Drew argued that Lockwood was the bigger problem, a vain city man misreading everyone he met, and Colton found he could not entirely disagree, which unsettled him more than disagreement would have. If both narrators distorted, then the reader was left triangulating, and what he wanted, what the essay demanded, was a verdict. Trust or don't trust. He had assumed analysis meant sharpening a question until it cut one way.

After the bell he stayed behind, pretending to organize a binder that needed no organizing. Ms. Reyes asked if he had a question. He said not exactly, then asked it anyway: whether an essay could argue that you trust Nelly about some things and not others, that she might be accurate about weather and dishonest about motives, and whether that counted as an answer or just a refusal to choose.

She smiled and said the prompt asked who he trusted, not how much.

On the bus home he opened his notebook under the fogged window and wrote the word "scale" at the top of the page. Trust, he was beginning to think, was not a door you opened or kept shut; it was something with sentience of its own, an attention you paid in increments, adjusting as the evidence adjusted. He could not say that in an essay, or not in those words. But he could take the scene where Nelly watches Catherine through a keyhole and Heathcliff watches through the same keyhole, hearing two people he loves say two incompatible things about him, and he could ask what Nelly chose to keep, and what Lockwood chose to laugh at, and where the reader's own keyhole had been all along. He underlined a line of dialogue in the chapter, closed the book, and watched the houses slide past, each one holding, he supposed, somebody's version of the truth.

He got off two stops early and texted his mother: ask Uncle Ray about Thanksgiving 2016. Then he stood at the crosswalk, thumb still over the send button, and waited for the light.

The open house on Marsden Street was Blake's idea before it was his mother's, which surprised them both. He had seen the listing at eleven the night before, a flat above a shuttered bakery with a letting agent's name he didn't recognise, and by morning he had talked her into driving over, mostly because he wanted to see what £725 a month actually looked like when it stood in front of you as a room. The agent, a man named Dev with a lanyard and a folding table, was halfway through telling a young woman about the deposit when Blake and his mother came up the stairs.

"Two months up front," Dev was saying. "That's the deposit, plus your first month's rent in advance. Standard practice."

The woman, who introduced herself to nobody in particular as Priya, had a folder of printouts under her arm. She was maybe twenty-two, twenty-three, with the particular tiredness of someone who had viewed six flats this week. "Two months," she repeated, in a voice that suggested she had heard this number before and disliked it more each time.

"That's right." Dev had begun to pontificate about landlords needing security, about people who damaged properties, about the market being what it was, and Blake could see Priya's attention sliding off him the way his own did when a teacher covered material he already knew was beside the point.

She opened her folder. "The flat's £900 a month," she said. "That's under fifty thousand a year. So the deposit can't be two months. It's capped at five weeks' rent. I checked last night, the Tenant Fees Act 2019." She said it plainly, not triumphantly, the way you'd read out a bus timetable.

Dev's mouth opened and then reconsidered. Behind him, another couple had paused at the folding table, listening. "Five weeks," he said slowly, as if weighing a stone in his hand. "Right. Let me just call the office."

Blake drifted toward the kitchen while Dev stepped onto the landing with his phone. His mother followed, running her finger along the windowsill the way she did in every property they entered, an audit she performed without thinking. Blake had been doing the arithmetic since the listing: £725 a month, a deposit of five weeks, which meant five sevenths of a month's rent, which meant roughly £518. He did it again on his phone to be sure. And then the other number, the one that had brought him here in the first place: his mother's mention, three weeks ago and half a glass of wine into the evening, that she'd never owned, that she'd been paying other people's mortgages for twenty years.

"Mum," he said quietly, "if we put our rent money toward a deposit instead, what would that even take?"

She didn't stop looking at the windowsill. "A down payment, you mean. Different thing from a deposit, though everyone mixes them up. You pay a deposit to borrow a flat. A down payment buys you a stake in one." She turned around. "Ten percent, usually, for a first-time buyer with a mortgage. On a small place around here, that's fifteen, eighteen thousand."

Blake let the number sit. He had £2,400 saved from two summers of shelf-stacking, which had previously felt like a lot of money and now felt like a paragraph of a much longer book. "So the landlord's been collecting our rent for years," he said, "and that's been paying off his mortgage, and at the end we have nothing."

"That's the arrangement," his mother said. "It's not a betrayal. It's just what rent is." But she said it while looking at the little garden through the kitchen window, a strip of concrete with a stubborn rosemary bush in a pot, and Blake understood that explaining a thing and accepting it were not the same act.

On the landing, Dev came back in with the flattened posture of a man overruled by his own office. "Five weeks it is," he said to Priya. "I'll amend the paperwork. In advance, that's the first month's rent still, but the deposit comes down." Priya nodded and wrote the numbers in her folder, and Blake watched her do it, this small correction of a system by one person with a printout, and felt something adjust in his chest that he couldn't yet name.

He thought about his grandfather, who lived with a kind of grandiose asceticism, refusing heating in winter and calling it character while filling the house with enormous ornate furniture nobody could sit on. Saving money and wasting it, all at once, in the name of a story he told himself. Blake suspected the housing market had a bit of that in it too, people spending enormous sums to feel a certain way about themselves, landlords and tenants both.

Outside, Priya was on the steps, and Blake caught up with her before he'd decided to. "That thing you said, about five weeks," he said. "Would you send me where you found it? I'm trying to work all this out and I don't know anyone who's done it."

She looked at him, sixteen and earnest in his school coat, and something in her expression softened. "I'll send the link," she said. "Half the battle is knowing the rules exist. The other half I haven't worked out yet." She pulled her folder tight under her arm and started down the street toward the bus stop, and Blake stood on the steps with his mother's car keys in his hand, adding five weeks and ten percent and £2,400 together in his head, and then took out his phone and made a note of the number he got.

Hayden had been carrying the folded printout in his blazer pocket for three days, and by graduation morning the paper had gone soft at the creases, the way money does.

The hallway outside the gym smelled of floor wax and carnations. He stood at his locker for the last time, turning the dial out of habit even though the locker was already empty, and Dana from his econ class stopped beside him with her cap mashed flat under one arm.

"You're still on about the wages thing," she said. It wasn't a question. Dana had spent the year building a spreadsheet of every scholarship in the state, and she wanted his essay in the class anthology because it had made their teacher, Mr. Ruiz, actually sit down.

"My uncle said it at dinner Friday," Hayden said. "He works at the community college. He told me workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma earned eight ninety-nine a week, median, in 2023, and people without one earned seven oh eight." He recited it the way he'd recited it to himself in the shower, in the car, in the dark before sleep. "He said, that's your present, kid. That's what the paper's worth."

"That's not what the paper's worth," Dana said, but she didn't say what it was worth, and he noticed that.

The problem was that Hayden had written his exit essay, the one Mr. Ruiz had read aloud in April, about how a diploma measured nothing, how the whole ceremony was theater, a kind of polite nihilism dressed in robes. He'd been proud of the anger in it. Now the anger had a number attached, a small one, a hundred and ninety-one dollars a week, and the number refused to be romantic. He tried to transcribe the essay's argument into his notebook on the bench by the trophy case, to see whether it survived contact with what his uncle had said, and found that his own sentences looked petulant to him, a boy throwing his cap at the floor because the floor existed.

"Ruiz wants to read your name wrong," Dana said, watching him write. "He told me. He's been practicing."

"He won't read it wrong. It's two syllables."

"He reads everything wrong. He called me Dana with a hard E for a month." She fixed her cap on her head, crooked on purpose, because Dana wanted the yearbook photographer to catch it, wanted one image from the day that hadn't been arranged by adults. "My mother wants the cap straight. My whole family's coming straight-ward today. I'm the crooked element."

He laughed, and then the doors opened and the gym swallowed them, and the ceremony went the way ceremonies go, long and warm and strange. Mr. Ruiz did read his name wrong, "Hay-den" like two separate words, and Hayden walked the length of the gym with his hand out for a diploma case that turned out to be empty, a holder, the real one to be mailed in July after the office confirmed his detention hours had been served. He held it up anyway. His mother stood up in the third row and took a picture, and later he found the picture showed the case's emptiness clearly, the little window with nothing behind it, and he understood that his uncle's numbers and his own essay had both been about this case, one saying it was worth eight ninety-nine a week and the other saying it was worth nothing, and both of them talking about a piece of cardboard that hadn't even arrived.

Afterward, in the hallway, the one from that morning, now scattered with programs and a dropped carnation, his uncle found him. Uncle Marcel had the community college lanyard still on, though it was Saturday.

"So," Marcel said. "You got the eight ninety-nine version or the seven oh eight version?"

"Neither yet," Hayden said. "They mail it."

Marcel grinned, then didn't. "You know I wasn't trying to put a price on it. I was trying to say it matters. There's a difference."

"I know," Hayden said, and found that he did, mostly. What he couldn't say, what stayed uncertain even as he reached for it, was whether the diploma mattered because of the money or the money because of the diploma, or whether both of those were smaller than something his essay had been circling without landing on. He had spent a year learning to argue one side of things. Nobody had taught him how to hold two true sentences at once.

Dana appeared with her cap still crooked, holding her phone at arm's length. "The photographer got it," she said. "Look. My grandmother is frowning at me in the background and my mom is mid-yell. It's perfect. It's the only real picture anyone took today." She turned the screen toward Hayden and his uncle together, two witnesses, as if the picture needed certifying.

Hayden looked at it, the crooked cap, the frowning grandmother, the half-open gym doors behind them all, and thought that this was what he'd write next, if he wrote anything. Not that nothing mattered. Not that anything could be priced.

"So what's it going to be, kid," Marcel said, clapping him on the shoulder. "College or the seven oh eight?"

"College," Hayden said, and then, because the hallway was almost empty and the honest thing was easier out loud, "I don't know what for."

Marcel pulled the lanyard over his head and dropped it in Hayden's blazer pocket, right on top of the soft folded number. "Hold onto that too," he said. "It's worth exactly nothing a week."

Noah's first paycheque sat folded in his back pocket through the whole dinner shift, and between clearing plates he kept touching it the way you touch a sore tooth. He had worked thirty-one hours at Palmer's Grill over three weeks, and he had done the math in his head a dozen times: minimum wage times thirty-one, close to four hundred dollars. The cheque was for three hundred and eight.

The kitchen smelled of burnt butter and dish steam. He stacked plates too fast, chipped one, and slid it to the back of the rack where nobody would see. His plan had been simple. He needed two hundred and eighty for the used amp that Marcus was selling before he moved to Edmonton, and Marcus had said Friday, no later, because he needed the money for the move. Friday was tomorrow. Noah had counted on the cheque covering it with room to spare.

Under the fluorescents in the staff room, during his break, he unfolded the stub and read it slowly. Gross pay, four hundred and nine. Then lines he hadn't expected: CPP, EI, income tax. Each one small, but together they had eaten over a hundred dollars, and the income tax line was the strangest of all, because it said he would probably get most of it back in the spring, on something called a return. Money taken, then possibly returned. He understood that it was legal, since everyone at school who had jobs complained about it, but legal and fair were not the same word, and he wasn't sure yet which one this was.

What he did next felt less like curiosity than like gathering evidence. In the staff room there was a corkboard of old receipts the accountant had pinned up, and Noah pulled one from a supplier order and compared it to the customer bills in his apron. On the supplier receipt there was a separate line, GST five percent, added at the bottom. On the food bills there was nothing like it, because the tax was already inside the menu prices, or at least that was what he gathered from the way the totals worked out. He was still turning this over when the door chimed and a family came in, the father speaking with a flat, rounded accent that made Noah think of late-night television.

He took their order, brought the bread basket, and when he set down the bill the father squinted at it and then at his phone, where he had pulled up a photograph of a restaurant receipt from home. "Yours hides it," the man said to his wife, not quietly. "Back home there's VAT, twenty percent, and it's been that since the fourth of January, 2011." He tapped the photo. "Built into the price, but it's on the receipt, spelled out." Noah, clearing the next table, heard every word.

Later, at home, he looked it up on his laptop to be sure, because one overheard sentence wasn't evidence. It checked out, and he fell down a small rabbit hole of British receipts and Canadian ones, side by side, until his eyes ached. It seemed to him that there were two honest ways to do it: show the tax, or build it in. Marcus, over text, expatiated on the topic for six long messages, arguing that hidden taxes were endemic to governments everywhere, that they took your money in the dark so you'd stop noticing. Noah typed and deleted three replies. It wasn't exactly the dark. The number was right there on the stub, itemized, and on the UK receipt, itemized, and on the supplier's bill, itemized. Whether it felt like theft or like the price of roads and hospitals seemed, tonight, like a question of semantics dressed up as a principle. He wasn't ready to pick a side of that argument, and he noticed he didn't trust anyone who already had.

The withheld thing, the thing he hadn't told Marcus, was that the cheque was already spent in his mind. In the morning he would have to decide whether to ask his mother for a loan, which meant explaining the deductions, which meant admitting he'd expected four hundred and hadn't read anything about payroll before taking the job. He rehearsed it at the kitchen table while she stirred soup. "They take income tax off every cheque," he said, "but most of mine comes back on a return, because I won't earn enough this year to owe it. The other stuff, CPP and EI, that's gone for now." She nodded slowly, watching him. "So the number they advertise as your wage isn't your wage," she said. "Right," Noah said, and then, more carefully, "but it's not a lie either."

She lent him eighty dollars, and he made the handoff to Marcus in the school parking lot at lunch, the amp heavy and cold through his jacket. Marcus counted the bills, and Noah watched him count, and thought about how much of every dollar in Marcus's palm had already been taxed before it reached his hand, and how much would be taxed again when Marcus spent it, and how little of that either of them would ever see written down. "You okay?" Marcus asked. Noah hefted the amp into his locker. "Yeah," he said. "Carry it for me. It's heavier than it looks."

Sebastian had agreed to spend the last week of August at his grandparents' house on the condition that he could use the darkroom in the basement, which his grandfather had built in 1974 and never dismantled. The application to art school was due in November, and the requirement that frightened him most was not the ten artworks but the statement, the single page in which he was supposed to explain what held them together. He had chosen self-portraits as his theme, mostly because he had a camera and no other subject, and already the problem had revealed itself: on his third day, tacking contact sheets to the corkboard above the drying rack, he counted eight versions of the same narrow face squinting into the same lens.

"Your grandfather kept saying you'd find it down there," his grandmother called from the top of the stairs. She had her own project that week, a stack of his grandfather's framed prints she wanted to sort through and donate to the library, and she wanted Sebastian's opinion on which ones. He heard her slippers scuffing on the linoleum above him for hours at a time, the particular hush of someone preserving something.

Between trays of developer he wandered the shelves. His grandfather had been a genuine aesthete, a man who arranged even his WD-40 and his masking tape with a curator's care, and the art books were ordered by decade. Sebastian pulled down a heavy one with a black spine, opened it on the workbench beside the safelight, and stopped. Face after face, all the same woman, and none of them the same person: a secretary, a hitchhiker, a woman in a slip looking out a window as if the street below held a verdict. He checked the caption. Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.

He sat on the stool with the book open across his knees. Seventy, and every movie invented. She hadn't taken pictures of herself; she had taken pictures of a whole population that happened to share her face. Was that dishonest, or was it more honest than anything, since a person contains all those people anyway? He turned the pages slowly, wondering whether the woman in the slip had ever existed anywhere except in the moment the shutter opened, and deciding that maybe that was the only place anyone exists.

"Do you want soup or leftover chicken?" his grandmother called down that evening. He climbed the stairs with the book under his arm and found her at the kitchen table with the donation pile, three frames face down, two face up, a pencil tucked behind her ear like a carpenter. He noticed the pencil, the reading glasses pushed low, the small wet shine on one cheek she had not wiped.

"Grandpa had this," she said, tapping the cover. "He said it underpinned half of what people did with cameras afterward. I never liked them, honestly. All that pretending." She looked up. "Which of these should the library get? He'd have wanted you to choose."

He chose two for her, a foggy ferry dock and a portrait of her at thirty, and watched her hold that one a long moment before setting it aside from the donation pile, apart from the others, face up on the counter. She wanted him to take her to the library on Thursday to deliver them, and he said he would, and he did not say that Thursday was his deadline to mail the first draft of his statement.

In the darkroom the next morning he tried it. He put on his grandfather's gray cardigan and photographed himself at the window with a suitcase, then in his father's old work shirt with a toolbox, then simply as a boy looking at a darkroom door as if it led somewhere. The camera did not care who he was; it cared who he was pretending to be, and the pretending, he was starting to think, was not a mask over the truth but a way of auditing it. Still, the uncertainty stayed with him like the smell of fixer on his hands. Whether a portfolio of disguises added up to a self, or just to ten deflections from one, he could not yet say, and he wrote that sentence down and then crossed it out and then wrote it again.

Thursday morning he carried the framed ferry dock and the frame of his grandmother at thirty to the car while she locked the front door twice, the way she did. The artist's statement sat folded in his jacket pocket, one page, still provisional. In the passenger seat his grandmother rested the portrait of herself face down against her knees, then, as he backed out of the driveway, turned it over.

"Drive past the water before the library," she said. "Just once."

The art shed at Camp Wanoka smelled of cedar shavings and bug spray, and Lily had claimed the corner table by the window on the first day, which she now considered the single best decision of her summer. She was working on a drawing of the lake for the end-of-session exhibition, a wide panorama with the dock in the foreground and the far shore dissolving into hills. Her counselor had offered the campers a choice between painting and drawing, and Lily had chosen drawing because she wanted the picture to feel precise, the way a photograph feels precise, every plank of the dock distinct.

For three days it had gone well. Then the rain came, the humidity thickened, and the drawing began to smudge. The dark water of the lake spread its shadow upward into the sky whenever her sleeve crossed the paper, until it looked as though the hills were dissolving in a fog that had no business being there. She rubbed at it with a kneaded eraser and made it worse, a gray haze blooming across what had been clean white space.

"Which grade did you use?" asked Marcus, dropping onto the stool across from her. He was the boy from Cabin Four who drew dragons with obsessive detail, and he had a tin of pencils arranged like surgical instruments. Lily turned her pencil over and read the letter stamped on the barrel. "Six B, it says."

"That's your nemesis right there." He held up his own pencil, a thin pale thing. "A pencil's core is graphite mixed with clay. More clay makes it harder and lighter, and those are the ones marked H. Less clay makes it softer and darker, and those are marked B." He rolled the tin toward her. "You've basically been drawing with charcoal wearing a disguise."

Lily sat with that for a moment. She had always assumed darkness was simply a matter of pressing harder, that effort itself made the mark. The idea that darkness was built into the tool, decided before her hand ever moved, bothered her in a way she could not immediately name. She picked up an H pencil and made a test stroke on the corner of a scrap. The line was so faint she had to tilt the paper toward the window to see it, pale as a hair, and when she dragged her thumb across it, nothing smudged at all.

She thought of her grandmother's kitchen table, where she had learned to draw at seven or eight, sprawled across the vinyl tablecloth with a single soft pencil from a junk drawer. Her grandmother had never taught her anything about materials; she had only slid biscuits across the table and said, "Draw the sugar bowl, sweetheart, draw it just as it is." Lily had pressed and pressed to get the shadow under the bowl dark enough, tearing the paper once, and her grandmother had laughed and said the shadow could be whatever color Lily wanted, because drawings weren't under oath. That had felt like freedom then. She had never thought to ask whether a different pencil existed.

Now she laid the two test strokes side by side on the scrap, the deep feathered smear of the 6B and the disciplined whisper of the H, and she understood that neither one was the true one. The hard pencil gave her the control she wanted for the dock planks and the far hills; the soft one gave her the weight of the water and the mass of the pines. She had been trying to codify her whole drawing into a single method, one way of making a mark, when the panorama needed both. She began the lake over again on fresh paper, blocking the sky and water with the 6B in loose sweeps, then trading it for an H to pick out the dock, its railing, the far shoreline, letting the hills stay half-suggested.

It was slow, and it was not clean. Sometimes she pressed the soft pencil too hard where the hard one belonged, and the bank of the lake blurred again, and she lifted the paper and blew across it and kept going. Marcus drifted back after dinner and watched without comment, an epicurean silence about him, savoring her struggle the way he savored the precise suffering of getting a dragon's wing membrane right. He did reach over once and rotate her paper so her sleeve would stop crossing the wet graphite, and she said thanks without looking up.

On the last night before the exhibition, the drawing was finished in the only sense that mattered to her, which was that she had stopped. The lake held its darkness without bleeding into the sky, and the hills were pale and far, and the dock stood crisp and quiet above the water. She tacked it to the exhibition board between a painted canoe and Marcus's dragon, stood back, and found that she still did not know whether the picture was good, or only finished, and that the two might not be the same thing, and that she could live with not knowing. Marcus came and stood beside her, arms crossed, studying the dock.

"Which one is that," he said, "the H or the B?"

Lily pointed at the hills, then at the water, and said, "Both."

The seats were high enough that the whole field lay open below Julia like a diagram, the players reduced to careful marks moving along chalked lines. Her father sat on her left with his program rolled into a tube, and on her right Deshawn kept leaning forward to argue with her uncle two rows down, though neither of them could hear the other over the crowd. The dispute had started in the second quarter, when the running back stretched for the end zone and the ball came loose a breath before his knee touched. The officials had called it a touchdown. Deshawn's family, loyal to the other side, had not stopped shouting since.

"He was in," her father said, for the fourth time.

"You're circumscribing the whole argument to one angle," Julia said. "From here you can't see where the ball is. Nobody can. That's the point." She was surprised at herself for saying it, because an hour ago she had been the one screaming that it was a fumble, certain of it, certain in the way the crowd makes you certain, as if fifty thousand voices agreeing could substitute for seeing.

The stadium scoreboard showed the call standing and then went dark, offering nothing. Around them, people were pulling out their phones, holding them up like torches, and a man behind them kept repeating that they should show it again, the way they always do on television, just show it again and everyone would know. Julia pulled out her own phone, and because the signal was sluggish, and because the argument had begun to feel like something she wanted to settle rather than win, she typed a question into the search bar instead of checking the score.

What she found made her sit still. The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by a director named Tony Verna. She read it twice. It had happened in this sport, in a stadium like this one, and it had not always existed. There had been a first time, a person who built it, a date. Her whole life the replay had been there, sedimentary, layered so deep beneath every game she'd watched that she had never once thought of it as something someone invented.

She tapped Deshawn's shoulder. "When was the first instant replay ever shown on television?"

"Like the technology? I don't know. The seventies?"

"CBS. December 7, 1963. The Army-Navy game. A director named Tony Verna devised the system."

Deshawn squinted at her. "Sixty-three? So before that people just argued?"

"Forever, probably. That's all there was." Julia looked down at the field, where the teams were lining up again, and felt the ground shift a little under her certainty. If her grandfather had watched that game, he had lived in a world where a blown call was simply final, where you went home with the argument unsettled and it stayed unsettled. She had assumed that the truth of the play was available, that it was only a matter of showing it, and maybe it was, but the fact that the showing itself was an invention made her wonder what else she treated as natural. The officials had seen more angles than anyone in her section. That didn't make them right. It meant only that their blindness was different.

"Okay, but they're going to review it upstairs," Deshawn said. "It's not 1963 anymore."

"That's true," Julia said. "But we're up here. Whatever they decide, we'll take it on the same faith we'd have taken a coin flip sixty years ago." She realized she wasn't even sure anymore which outcome she wanted. Her father, meanwhile, had unrolled his program and was drawing the play from memory, marking the runner's path with a dotted line, and when Julia looked at his sketch she could see it both ways: the ball coming loose at the moment of the stretch, the knee a fraction behind. Her uncle turned around in his seat and jabbed a finger at the drawing.

"That dot's too far forward," he shouted over the noise. "He was a yard short."

"He wasn't," her father shouted back, and drew another dot.

Julia leaned between them, holding her phone out flat so they could both see the screen. "Before today, no one could have settled this," she said. "The first instant replay on television was CBS, the Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963, and the guy who devised the system was a director named Tony Verna." Her uncle blinked at it, then at her, and then the referee's voice boomed through the stadium, and every head in the section turned downward at once.

The call stands. Touchdown.

Deshawn whooped. Julia's father exhaled through his teeth, and after a moment he folded the program along the dotted line and put it in his coat. "I still think he was in," he said quietly, and handed her the pen.

Levi arrived at the Fairview Aquatic Center at 7:40 in the morning carrying a backpack that held, among other treasures, one whistle he had bought himself, a water bottle shaped like a shark, and absolutely no documentation of any kind.

"Orientation," said the assistant manager, Rosa, pointing at a folding table near the deep end. Four other teenagers sat there, all of them looking like they had been asked to defuse something. Rosa slid a paper across the table toward each of them. "You'll want to start on this."

Levi looked at his copy. It was a government form, dense and gray, and the part at the top was labeled Section 1. He read it twice. It wanted to know who he was, essentially, and whether the United States had agreed to let him be paid for existing.

"I thought orientation was like, where's the first aid kit," said the boy next to him, a lanky kid named Dominic who had introduced himself by claiming he could hold his breath for two minutes, a claim everyone at the table had silently agreed to never test.

"This has to be done today," Rosa said, checking her clipboard. "Section 1 of the Form I-9, no later than your first day of paid work. Everybody's first day is today, so." She said it lightly, the way you'd say the pool closes at eight, and walked off to argue with a vending machine.

Dominic flipped his form over as though the answers might be hiding on the back. "What happens if you just, don't?"

"I think you don't work," Levi said. "Like legally don't."

"My mom didn't say anything about a form." Dominic said this as though his mother had personally betrayed him. "She said bring a towel."

Levi filled out his name, which he managed without incident, and then reached the questions that required him to know things about himself he had never considered. Citizenship status. He checked the box for citizen, feeling briefly like he was voting. Then there was a spot for a signature and a date, and he signed with the pen he used for English homework, which ran out halfway through the L, so that his legal identity on file would forever be "Lev."

Rosa drifted back, still holding the vending machine's promise of a granola bar it had not delivered. "All good?"

"I have a question," Levi said. "Is this it, or is there more later? Because I don't have my passport or anything. It's in my dad's safe, which is where the passports live."

"That's Section 2, that's on us, you bring documents within a few days. Section 1 is yours, and it's due today." She rattled the granola bar free at last and looked triumphant about it, like she'd won a duel.

Dominic, meanwhile, had stopped writing entirely and was staring at the form with the expression of a boy watching his summer presaged into ruin. "I don't know my Social Security number."

"Nobody knows their Social Security number," said Priya, down the table. "It's like knowing your own blood type. People claim to, but they're lying."

"It's on my mom's phone," Dominic said. "My whole life is on my mom's phone."

By nine they had all finished, more or less, and Rosa led them out to the pool deck, where she explained the chair rotation and demonstrated a rescue tube with such enthusiasm that she nearly went in herself. The morning was warm and the water looked good enough to be misleading, and Levi climbed into the tall chair and felt, for one excellent minute, like exactly the person he had been pretending to be on the application.

During break he sat at the edge of the shallow end with his feet in the water and texted his older sister, Mara, who was at college and considered this a form of employment for herself, being texted.

His phone buzzed with her reply, which he read twice:

"Congratulations on being employable. An adage for you: dress for the job you want, which in your case is apparently a tank top and a fanny pack. Dad says your passport is in the safe and he'll bring the documents Thursday, also he says the safe combination is my birthday, which is a whole other conversation. Please do not rescue anyone your first day. Statistically you will not have to. Love you, do not get sued."

He texted back a shark emoji and then, because it felt like something she'd want to know, a sentence about the form: that every new employee has to complete Section 1 no later than their first day of paid work, which he had learned by being handed one and having no idea what it was.

Her reply came fast: "Look at you, learning labor law before learning to parallel park."

Dominic wandered over and sat down heavily, shoes and all, and put his feet in beside Levi's. "My mom's texting me my Social Security number in pieces so I don't get my identity stolen. She says it's like a ransom drop."

"Did you finish your form?"

"Yeah, I guessed the last two digits and then she corrected me." He tipped his head back toward the moribund vending machine, which stood in the corner looking like it had given up on commerce sometime in the previous decade. "You want to try the granola? Rosa says you have to hit it on the left side."

Levi pulled his feet out of the water, and the two of them walked over in their still-damp guard shirts, and he hit the machine on the left side exactly as instructed, and two granola bars fell at once.

"We split them," Dominic said.

"Obviously."

Behind them, somebody's kid cannonballed off the side where it clearly said no diving, and Levi grabbed his whistle off the bench and sprinted for the deck.

The line at First Meridian was eleven people long, and Juliette had memorized the back of the man in front of her: a gray fleece with a hole at the shoulder blade, a lanyard turned backward so his badge read in reverse. She was here to co-sign nothing, deposit her scholarship refund check, and, if she could manage it without crying, ask about the mortgage her grandmother kept mentioning like a riddle she expected Juliette to solve.

"Appointment?" the teller asked when Juliette finally reached the counter.

"Sort of. My grandmother's meeting with someone at two. I'm early." She slid the check under the glass. The teller stamped it with a satisfying thump, and Juliette watched her savings line tick upward by $1,847, which felt like a fortune until she remembered the apartment listings she'd been scrolling at midnight. Six hundred a month for a room with a slanted ceiling.
