The folding chair had her name on it, a strip of masking tape with CLAIRE V. in her principal's hurried print, and she sat down in the empty row of chairs an hour before anyone else would arrive. In her lap sat nine index cards, covered and recovered in her slanted handwriting, and the problem had not shrunk overnight. She could talk about resilience. She could talk about the future. Both options made her stomach turn, not because they were wrong but because they were borrowed, phrases worn smooth by every graduating class since the invention of folding chairs.

"Yo u up?" read the text from Dee, which was Dee's way of spelling "You're early." Claire texted back a photo of the chairs, the taped name, the white riser where the podium stood. "Coming," Dee wrote. "Don't abscond with my speech."

Dee was the salutatorian, a fact she had stopped pretending not to mind around March, when the final GPA had come down to a tenth of a point. She crossed the field now in the flat gray dress she'd argued about with her mother, carrying two coffees and her own cards, fewer than Claire's, held together with a rubber band. Her want was simple and she'd stated it plainly at lunch last week: she wanted to be funny. She'd spent three years being the smart one, the one teachers called on when no one else raised a hand, and she wanted, once, to make a whole stadium laugh on purpose.

"Read me the opening," Dee said, dropping into the chair beside her. Claire read it. Something about journeys and thresholds. Dee drank her coffee and said nothing, which in Dee's language was a verdict.

"I keep trying to write the ending," Claire said. "The goodbye part. And everything I write sounds like a greeting card ate a thesaurus. Like I'm performing erudition I don't actually have."

"So look it up. That's what you do." Dee tipped her chin at Claire's phone. "You're the one who found out the mascot was designed by a junior in 1974."

Claire already had the dictionary app open; that was the truth of it, she'd been typing before Dee finished the sentence. Valedictorian. She scrolled past the pronunciation, past the definition she knew, and found the etymology line near the bottom, small gray text under the entry.

"It comes from vale dicere," she read aloud. "Latin. It means 'to say farewell.' That's why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech. It's the whole job. I've been trying to write a speech about the future when the word itself is just asking me to say goodbye."

"Huh," Dee said, and stole one of Claire's index cards to write it down,vale dicere,in her rounder handwriting, and beneath it: "so it's not about being smart?"

The question sat between them longer than a question that size should. Because Claire had spent four years treating the title as a verdict, a number that proved something, and here was the word confessing that it had never been about that at all. It was about the leaving. The person with the highest grades had been assigned, by language itself, the task of standing up in front of everyone and admitting that this was over. She wasn't sure yet whether that was a relief or a heavier thing.

"So write the goodbye," Dee said. "Say what you'd actually miss. Not the building. Not the, like, hallowed halls."

"Marcus folding cheese pizza in half like a sandwich."

"The smell of the biology wing after the fetal pig unit."

They went on like that, trading specifics, and Claire wrote fast, filling a fresh card, then another. Somewhere in the middle of it she noticed the incipient ceremony assembling around them: a man on a ladder straightening the banner, the band hauling percussion up the riser steps, her grandmother's Buick pulling into the far lot, early the way her grandmother was early for everything, a woman who considered timeliness a form of love. Claire felt the strangest double pull, wanting the morning to stretch and wanting it over, and could not have said which wanting was stronger.

"Your turn to rehearse," she told Dee. "Show me funny."

Dee stood, cleared her throat at the empty stadium as if it were full, and delivered her opening line about the tenth of a point, a joke about how she'd asked the guidance office whether she could appeal it using attendance. The joke needed work. The delivery needed more work. But Dee grinned the whole way through, and somewhere out past center field a crow lifted off the goalpost and beat away over the treeline.

Claire looked down at her cards, the Latin copied twice in two hands. She still didn't know how to end the speech. She knew only that she would stand at that podium this afternoon and say farewell, in whatever clumsy words arrived, and that maybe the clumsiness was the point. She turned the taped chair around so the name faced her and said, quietly, "Vale."

The parking lot behind the closed hardware store had faded lines and one leaning light pole, and Savannah had chosen it because her mother would never think to look for her here. She sat in the driver's seat of the borrowed Corolla with her hands at ten and two, the way the pamphlet showed, while Mr. Okafor settled into the passenger seat and dropped a clipboard on his knee.

"I'm going to get my license before Labor Day," she said. "I have to. My brother's in a rehab place forty minutes out, and my mother works, and the visitation hours are two to four on Sundays." She had rehearsed the whole speech in the shower, and now it came out too fast, like she was afraid he would stop her.

Mr. Okafor buckled his seatbelt. "Turn the engine on first. Then we can litigate your Sunday plans."

She turned the key. The car shuddered awake under her, and she gripped the wheel harder than she needed to. For twenty minutes they did nothing but circles, wide lazy arcs around the light pole, her foot learning the small difference between the brake and the almost-brake. Twice she killed the engine and twice she restarted it without being told, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard both times, which she decided not to ask about.

"All right," he said finally. "Parking lot's done. We go on the road."

The road was a two-lane stretch behind the strip mall, empty enough at nine in the morning that she could hear her own pulse. She merged, sort of, and drove, and it was working, it was actually working, until she came up behind a delivery truck and realized she was close enough to read the phone number printed on its back doors. Her mother, who read contracts for a living and had once called Savannah's driving school contract "trenchant, in the way a dull knife is trenchant," would have said she was drafting a subpoena for a collision. Savannah eased off the gas but drifted forward again anyway, her foot convinced that closer meant safer, that if she could see the truck's mirrors the truck could see her.

"Don't slow down," Mr. Okafor said. "Just do something else. Watch the truck ahead of us. When it passes a fixed point, like that lamppost coming up, count seconds until we reach that same point."

"Why?"

"Try it. Out loud."

The truck's back bumper crossed the base of the lamppost. "One one-thousand, two one-thousand," she said, and her front bumper arrived at the same lamppost just after two. She checked the mirror. The gap between her and the truck looked enormous now, a whole polite room of empty pavement, and nothing bad had happened because of it. The truck hadn't escaped her. Nobody had honked. She tried it again at the next signpost, watching the truck pass the sign and counting, and got to three one-thousand before she reached it, and it still felt wrong, still felt like she was letting the world get ahead of her, but the wrongness was only in her foot, which kept wanting to close the gap like an apology.

"It's called the two-second rule," Mr. Okafor said, "in case anybody asks."

They drove to the end of the strip and back. Savannah held her count the whole way, at signs and mailboxes and a fire hydrant with a dented cap, and at a red light she sat with her hands still at ten and two and thought about her mother, who had spent the whole summer after Danny's arrest saying that if you loved people you stayed close to them, you stayed on their case, you did not let one inch open up between you. Savannah had believed her, had practically moved into Danny's room. But Danny had told her, the last visit, through plexiglass, that the inch was the only place he could breathe. She looked at the gap between her car and the truck idling ahead, counted it out of habit, three seconds, plenty, and thought that maybe you could hold on to people and still leave them room to move, though she couldn't have said where the holding stopped and the room began. That part she would have to work out the way she was working out the brake, by doing it and getting it wrong and doing it again.

"Same time Thursday," Mr. Okafor said when she parked, crooked but within the lines. "You'll count your way onto the highway."

"Thursday," she said. She was already planning the route to Danny's, every sign and lamppost along it, counting the seconds between her and everything ahead.

Logan's father backed the sedan into the far corner of the Kmart lot, where the painted lines had faded to the color of old bone, and cut the engine. "Switch," he said, and got out into the November wind without another word, which was his way of pretending this was ordinary.

It was not ordinary. Logan had waited since August, when his mother had taken him to the licensing office for the permit test and then, at the last minute, refused to come inside. She sat in the car with the heater running while he stood in line beneath a poster he read four times because the line barely moved. The poster said that according to the CDC, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. He had passed the test, walked out with the paper card in his fist, and slid into the passenger seat without mentioning the poster, and his mother had driven home on the far right of the road, both hands on the wheel, and said nothing either.

Now, four months later, his father tossed the keys across the roof of the car and Logan caught them against his chest. He adjusted the mirror too far, corrected it, adjusted it again. His father had already lowered the radio, which had been droning about inflation and stalled growth and something the commentator called stagflation, a word Logan filed away to look up later, though he gathered from context it meant prices climbing while the economy went nowhere, a kind of trap with no exit.

"Feet first," his father said. "Brake, then start it." Logan pressed the brake and the engine turned over and the whole car hummed around him like something alive that had merely been sleeping. He let off the brake too soon and they rolled an inch before he clamped down, and his father laughed, one short syllable, not unkind.

For half an hour it was only this: gas, brake, the wheel pulled in slow ovals around the empty cart corrals. Logan discovered that the car was parsimonious with information, telling him almost nothing until he asked with his hands and feet, and then telling him everything at once. His father said "wider" and "earlier" and once, quietly, "you're begging the wheel, don't beg it," and Logan understood that the machine could not be coaxed or beguiled into gentleness. It did exactly what he did, only larger.

"Pull up to that light pole and stop," his father said. "Then back around it." Logan lined up on the pole, checked the mirror his mother would have checked, and eased backward, and it was there, in the crooked slow arc of reverse, that the poster came back to him whole. Almost three times, per mile driven. He let the car stop and sat with his hands at ten and two.

"Dad," he said. "Did Mom see that poster at the DMV? The one about teen drivers." His father was quiet long enough that the ticking of the cooling engine became audible. "She stood outside last time because of it," he finally said. "August. You were inside taking the test and she was reading it through the window. She made me promise not to tell you."

Logan looked out at the empty lot, the cart corral, the light pole he had just circled without hitting. He thought of her silence on the drive home and had read it, all these months, as disappointment in him, and now he could not tell whether it had been fear instead, or whether the two were even separable. The numbers were the numbers. He was sixteen, and per mile he was more dangerous than his father, and no amount of care in this lot changed that yet; and still his mother had signed the permission slip, and still his father had driven him here, and both of those were also facts. "So she's been scared this whole time," Logan said, and it was not quite a question.

"She's been letting you drive anyway," his father said. "Same thing, sometimes." He pointed at the far end of the lot, where the empty spaces stretched out in long faded rows. "Take us down there. Full stop at the last line, and then home."

Logan checked the mirror, signaled out of habit into the emptiness, and pressed the gas.

Henry got the job the first week of June, which felt like a small miracle because he had assumed, all spring, that nobody would hire a sixteen-year-old who had never held anything resembling a position. The aquatic center hired him anyway, handed him a red whistle and a shirt two sizes too large, and put him in the tall chair by the deep end. He learned to watch the water the way his instructor had described it, in layers: the surface, where nothing was usually wrong, and beneath it, where everything could be.

By the middle of July he had stopped being nervous. He could spot an incipient panic from thirty feet away, a child whose strokes shortened and whose head bobbed a beat too fast, and he would slide down the ladder before the panic had a name. His mother said the job suited him. His father, who worked double shifts at the plant and considered rest a foreign country, said only, "Pick up hours when they offer them. You won't be sixteen forever."

So when the assistant manager, Dara, asked who could cover shifts during the county swim meet weekend, Henry raised his hand. He covered Marcus on Friday, covered two split shifts on Saturday, and came in Sunday for a birthday party of eleven eight-year-olds whose parents seemed to regard the lifeguard as a kind of rented conscience. By Sunday night his shoulders were sunburned and his legs ached from the ladder, and when he clocked out he counted the hours in his head and got forty-nine.

The paycheck came two Thursdays later. He read it standing at the mailbox in the wet heat, and the number was wrong, or rather it was wrong in a way that made it more right than he expected. The last several hours were paid at a higher rate than the rest, one and a half times what he usually made, as near as he could figure. He did the arithmetic twice on the back of a pool schedule he'd shoved in his back pocket. It checked out.

At work the next morning he found Dara at the front desk, sorting keys.

"Some of my hours were paid at a higher rate," he said. "Is that right?"

"Overtime," Dara said, not looking up. "Hours beyond forty in a workweek. One and a half times your regular rate. It's federal law for employees like us." She fished out a key, handed it to a man in a damp towel, and turned back. "Why, you didn't know?"

He hadn't. He had assumed that extra shifts meant extra money in a straight line, hour stacked on hour, and it had honestly never occurred to him that the law bent the line after forty. He felt something between gratitude and unease, the way he sometimes felt when a rule protected him for reasons he hadn't earned.

That afternoon, sitting in the tall chair, he thought about his father. His father spoke about the plant the way some people speak about the weather, as a thing that happened to him. Henry had heard him vilify management at dinner, then take a double the next day, and he had never understood how both could be true at once. Now he thought he saw it a little: his father worked the doubles because the money after forty was better money, and he resented that the better money existed only because the first forty had wrung him out. It was not hypocrisy. It was arithmetic with a wound in it.

Marcus climbed the ladder to relieve him at four. Marcus was nineteen, tanned, and indifferent to nearly everything except his car.

"You picked up the whole meet weekend," Marcus said, settling into the chair. "That's like a religious commitment. Lifeguard asceticism."

"It was forty-nine hours," Henry said.

"Saint Henry of the Deep End." Marcus blew the whistle at a kid running near the gutter, a short corrective blast. "I'd never do it. I did it one summer and stopped seeing my friends entirely. Money's money, but."

He said it lightly, the way people say things they mean more than they want to show. Henry looked at the water, which was calm, all layers of it, and considered that he had spent a weekend he would otherwise have spent with Eli and Sam at the creek, and that the check in his pocket had a number in it he liked, and that he could not yet tell which of those mattered more. He suspected the answer would change, and he suspected he would not always get to choose when.

Dara caught him at the gate as he left. "We need coverage again next weekend," she said. "Friday through Sunday. There's a meet."

Henry stood with his hand on the chain link, the whistle still warm in his pocket.

"Can I take just Friday?" he said. "Just the one day?"

Dara shrugged and wrote it on the clipboard. Behind her, the pool lay flat and bright, and a kid on the diving board was counting his toes in preparation for something reckless.

The decision was supposed to post at five o'clock, which meant Abigail spent seventh period in Mr. Okafor's Human Geography class with her phone face-down in her backpack and her heart rate somewhere near the ceiling. The room smelled like dry-erase marker and the oranges Marcus peeled every day without fail, dropping the rind in a slow pile beside his map of Central Asia. Mr. Okafor was drawing the Eurasian steppe on the board, a long flat grassland he shaded in green, and Abigail copied it into her notes without processing a single word.

Marcus leaned over during the worksheet. "You're writing steppe on top of Poland," he said.

"Am I."

"You've written it four times. Abigail."

She looked down. Four steppes, stacked like sedimentary layers across Eastern Europe, each one slightly crooked. She crossed them out. At five o'clock the portal would either show a word like congratulations or a word like regret, and everything she'd done for four years had already been boiled down to whichever one appeared, and no amount of knowing that was unreasonable made it stop being true.

"Hey," Marcus said, quieter. "Remember March."

"March," she said.

"When you took the SAT. You came out of that room looking like you'd seen a ghost. You told me the second math module was brutal."

She remembered it exactly. The testing room had been cold enough that her fingers slipped on the trackpad, and when the harder questions started stacking up, question after question she couldn't immediately untangle, she had been certain she was failing. She'd ridden home on the bus constructing an apology to her parents.

"And then I told you," Marcus said. "It's adaptive now. Since March of 2024, the SAT in the U.S. is digital, and it adapts. How you do on the first module of each section sets how hard the second module is. So if the second one felt impossible, that probably meant you'd earned the hard one. You did well enough on the first module that the test gave you the tough second." He tapped her worksheet. "And then your score came back and you screamed in the cafeteria and made a senior drop his pizza."

"I didn't make him drop it."

"You made him drop it."

She had gotten a 780 in math, a number no one could impugn, and she had felt, for about a week, like a person the world made sense to. Then she'd written her essays and hit submit and gone back to being a person checking her email eleven times a day. The adaptive test had at least been legible. Work hard on module one, receive module two, read the difficulty of your own future off the difficulty of your questions. Colleges were not adaptive. Colleges made you wait five weeks and then posted all decisions at the same hour on the same Friday, and gave you no module two at all.

The clock said 2:47. Mr. Okafor moved on to rain shadow deserts. Marcus went back to his worksheet, and the oranges sat in their rind pile, and someone's pencil case zipper went up and down three times in the back row.

At 3:31, in study hall, her phone buzzed once, face-up this time because she'd given up on dignity. An email from the admissions office. Not the decision, she realized after her stomach had already dropped; a notice that decisions would post at 5:00 as planned, with a link to the portal and a sentence thanking applicants for their patience. Abigail laughed out loud, alone at a library table, a short ugly bark that made the boy across from her look up from his flashcards.

At 5:04 she was home, on the floor of her room with the laptop actually on her lap, because sitting in a chair felt too casual for the occasion. The portal took forty seconds to load. The screen was pale and the fan hummed against her knees the whole time.

The word was "deferred." Not congratulations, not regret. We have not yet reached a final decision on your application, the letter said, and we will revisit it in the spring.

She sat there while the fan hummed. She had done well on the first module, she thought, and she had done well on the second, and the test had told her so with numbers, and this told her nothing except wait. There was no reading the difficulty of this off anything. Marcus texted a picture of the steppe worksheet with the word LOL under her four crooked crossings-out.

She typed back, "deferred," and then, before she could decide whether it was a joke, "the questions got harder. so I must be doing great."

From downstairs her mother called that dinner was in ten minutes. Abigail closed the laptop, and the room went quiet except for the fan winding down.

I had always been careful with lists, and this one was no exception: eleven colleges, ranked, with columns for average aid, distance from home, and whether they had a real Classics department, because I had decided, sometime in October, that I was going to be a polymath, a person who read Latin and coded in Python and could not be reduced to a single line on a resume. My brother Theo said that was just a fancy word for being unable to choose, but Theo was thirteen and believed this was a character flaw.

I sat at the kitchen computer because my laptop had died in November, and because the kitchen was where my mother was, wrapping candle orders for her holiday rush. The Common App glowed in front of me, seven of eleven applications done, and I told myself I did not care about the money part, which was, I understand now, the first thing I got wrong. I believed I had arranged everything so that finances were not the deciding factor. I had even told my college counselor, Ms. Okafor, that I refused to let money pick my school, as though refusing to look at something made it disappear.

"Which ones are left?" my mother asked, not looking up from her tissue paper.

"Carver, Halstead, Ryland, and Dupre," I said. "The good ones."

"The expensive ones," she said, mild, and I said, "Aid exists, Mom," in the voice I used when I wanted a subject closed. She let it close. That was her way; she noticed when I was gripping the mouse too hard and simply set a mug of tea at my elbow without comment.

Carver I submitted in ten minutes, my essay about translating Catullus at the laundromat already uploaded. Halstead took longer because Halstead wanted an extra paragraph on "intellectual curiosity," a phrase I found nearly meaningless. It was while fact-checking a statistic about Halstead's Classics department that I found the thread that unraveled everything: a forum post from a student saying that at some schools, applying for financial aid actually affected your chances of admission. I had assumed the opposite, obviously, because it would be monstrous otherwise, because money should not get to vote on your worth.

I clicked through to a table on a college data site and cross-checked it twice. Some colleges were need-blind, meaning they decided whom to admit without ever considering whether the applicant could afford to pay. Many others, and this was the part that made my ears go hot, were need-aware instead, which meant they did look. I checked the table against my list. Ryland and Dupre, my two remaining reaches, the ones I had been calling my dreams since September, were need-aware. Halstead, which I had just submitted with a financial aid application attached, was need-aware too.

"Mom," I said. "Do you know what need-blind means?"

She came over, hands still dusty with tissue paper, and read the screen. "No," she said. "Tell me."

"It means they admit you without looking at whether you can pay. Some schools do that. A lot of them don't." Saying it out loud, I heard how naive my earlier confidence had been, all that October certainty about not letting money decide, as if I had been the one in control. I had built my list on prestige and Latin and weather, and had never once checked this column, because checking it felt like admitting what we were, and I did not want our finances to be something that could stigmatize me even on paper. That was the second thing I got wrong, and it was worse than the first.

Theo wandered in, saw my face, and asked if somebody died. "Nobody died," I said. "I have to redo my list." And that, in the end, was what I did, though redoing is too tidy a word for it. I spent two hours at the kitchen table with the table printed out, my mother drying mugs beside me, moving Ryland and Dupre from the dream column to the honest column, where they stayed, because being need-aware did not make them villains and did not make me a charity case; it made them a risk I could see instead of one I couldn't. I added three need-blind schools I had dismissed as boring, and one of them, it turned out, had a scholar program for exactly the kind of unfocused, voracious reader I actually was, the kind Theo mocked. The worry that students like me, patching together aid, were somehow an underclass at the fancy schools, that this anxiety was endemic rather than particular to me, was a worry I could name now but not settle. I would not know until March whether any of it mattered.

At eleven, my mother went to bed and Theo left his half-finished algebra homework on the counter, a small surrender. I reopened the Common App, read my Catullus essay once more, and pressed submit on the first of the need-blind schools, then sat listening to the modem-shaped silence that follows.

The drive down from Silverton took an hour and a half, long enough for the last of her battery to bleed out somewhere past the reservoir, so Vanessa walked into the phone store holding a dead black rectangle instead of a phone. The town where she lived was small and montane, a shelf of houses pinned between two ridgelines, and the nearest store that sold anything was down here in the valley, in a strip mall between a nail salon and a credit union. Her phone was four years old. The battery had been dying by noon since spring, and yesterday it had shut itself off during her college interview, mid-sentence, while a woman on a screen in Denver waited for her to finish an answer about the book that had changed her life.

She had two hundred and twelve dollars, most of it from a summer bussing tables, sitting in an account at that credit union her grandmother had opened when Vanessa turned fifteen. The phone she wanted, the one with the camera good enough for the photography elective she'd been admitted to, cost seven hundred ninety-nine. A clerk named Deshawn, who kept a desiccated little cactus on the counter behind the register and clearly hadn't watered it in a year, slid a glossy card across the glass. Financing, he said. No money down, twenty-four payments, and she could walk out with the phone today. He smiled when he said today, the way people smile when they're handing you something.

Vanessa asked what the payments were. He turned the card over and pointed at a table of numbers, small ones at first, and she did what she did in math class, which was multiply. Twenty-four of this, plus an origination fee, plus a rate that got added because she was seventeen and had never borrowed anything and would need her mother to co-sign. The total came out to more than seven hundred ninety-nine. Not catastrophically more, but more, and when she asked why, Deshawn said, "That's the interest. That's how lending works. You're paying for the use of their money over time." He said it kindly, without any speech attached, and turned to help a man in a Carhartt jacket who was tapping a display phone with one finger like it might be fake.

While she waited she drifted next door, partly for something to do and partly because the credit union had a rack of pamphlets by the door and she was seventeen with two hundred and twelve dollars and a phone problem, which is to say she was in the mood to look at anything with numbers on it. A brochure about savings accounts for members under eighteen showed two options side by side. Both paid three percent. One compounded monthly, one yearly, and at the bottom, in faint gray print the size of ants, was the formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). Under it, a note the designer had probably been told to include and had done so as unobtrusively as possible: n is the number of times per year interest is added.

She borrowed a pen from the counter. She had no calculator, because her calculator was a dead phone, so she worked it out longhand on the back of a deposit slip, slowly, checking herself. Five hundred dollars, three percent, one year, annual compounding: five hundred times one point zero three, five hundred fifteen. Then the monthly one. Three percent divided by twelve, that tiny fraction, raised to the twelfth power. She multiplied it out digit by digit, and the answer was five hundred fifteen dollars and a bit of change. More than the other one. Not by much, a dollar and change on five hundred, but more, and the difference came from nothing except how often they added the interest. She sat with that for a second. The same rate, the same year, and the money that got touched twelve times came out slightly ahead.

So here was what she knew, standing between the two buildings. If she borrowed, seven hundred ninety-nine would quietly become more than seven hundred ninety-nine, the way water runs downhill, without her ever feeling it leave. If she saved, two hundred and twelve would become slightly more than two hundred and twelve, the way a plant grows, also without her feeling it. The two facts faced each other in her head like people on opposite benches, and she couldn't make them shake hands. One said walk out with the phone today. The other said the future version of her, the one in college, would be either slightly richer or slightly poorer depending on this afternoon, and that version of her was the one who needed the camera.

She went back into the phone store. Deshawn was free now, and she set her dead phone on the counter and asked what it would cost to just replace the battery. He turned it over, looked at the swelling along the back seam, and winced. Fifty-five dollars, and he could have it done in an hour. She heard herself say okay before she had fully decided, and then she stood at the counter sliding her card into the reader for the fifty-five, watching the little hourglass, and her stomach tightened because she was suddenly unsure, for no reason she could name, whether the two hundred and twelve was all still there, whether the overdraft from the book she'd ordered in August had ever actually cleared.

The screen read APPROVED. She let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding.

"The savings account," she said, while Deshawn pried the back off her phone, "the one that compounds monthly. Can you switch somebody into that from here?"

"Wrong building," he said, not looking up. "But it's twenty feet."

"I know where it is," Vanessa said, and picked up the dead phone, and the pen she still hadn't returned, and walked out toward the double doors with the deposit slip folded in her fist.

The house smelled like paint and nothing else, and Emile stood in the middle of the living room holding a phone with no signal bars, listening to it ring anyway. His mother had driven to the old town that morning to collect the last box from the old house, which meant he had six hours alone in a building where his footsteps sounded like someone else's. On the third ring, Danny picked up.

"You're calling from the future," Danny said. "How's the future?"

"Empty. There's a fridge with one water bottle in it and a floor I could sleep on." Emile sat down on the floor to prove it, cross-legged, the phone on speaker between his knees. Danny was telling him about Priya's party, the one Emile had known he would miss the moment the moving truck door rolled down, and Emile found he was listening less to the words than to the background noise of a kitchen he had eaten in maybe two hundred times. When the call dropped he sat there a while, and when he tried to introspect, to look squarely at what he was feeling, the honest answer was smaller than he expected. Not grief. Something more like vertigo, the feeling of a step that isn't there.

He went out through the garage because the front door still had no screen, and that was how he met the neighbor. She was crouched at the end of her driveway, pulling tape off a cardboard box marked BOOKS, and she looked up and said, "You're the new ones. Nobody's lived in that house since the Hendersons, and that was two years." Her name was Ruth Okafor, and this was, technically, the second time they had met; she had waved once from her porch on moving day, and Emile had waved back, and neither of them had crossed the street.

She asked what he was doing with himself all summer before college, and he said nothing much, and she said, "That's a waste of a waste," which made no sense until she explained she owned the garden shop on Delancey and needed someone for the register and the watering, mornings, and could he start Thursday. He said yes before he had decided to. Walking back across the street he kept turning it over. In the old town it had taken him a year to get a job at the pool, and that was only because Danny's sister worked there. He had known Ruth Okafor for four days, one of them only as a wave.

That night he texted Priya: I got a job from the neighbor I've met twice. She replied with a screenshot, some article his old history teacher had apparently posted, with the line highlighted: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper "The Strength of Weak Ties" found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. "Mr. Halloran says this is you," she wrote. Emile read it twice, then looked it up himself, squinting at his phone in the bare room, sitting on an air mattress with his back against the wall.

It rearranged something. All through senior year he had believed that the friends you had were the whole architecture of your life, that leaving them was leaving everything, and here was evidence that the people at the edges, the waved-at neighbors, the classmates he never quite talked to, did things his closest friends could not. He thought about how Priya had gotten her bookstore job, through a woman her mother played tennis with, someone Priya had met maybe twice, and how nobody had remarked on it, because nobody remarked on the obvious. He wanted to call Danny and lay it all out, and he picked up the phone and then set it down, because it wasn't the kind of thing Danny would want a lecture about, and because Emile wasn't sure yet what he actually thought.

Thursday morning he watered forty flats of impatiens wrong, flooding three of them, and Ruth showed him again without raising her voice. At ten a woman came in looking for something virulent, her word, to kill the moss on her bricks, and Ruth steered her to a product and then, after the woman left, said, "People always want the harshest thing for the smallest problem." Emile wrote that down mentally, or thought he did. His discernment about plants was nonexistent; he couldn't tell a weed from a seedling, and twice he pulled things Ruth had to rescue. But by the second week he could run the register, and he knew the names of four regulars, and one of them, a man named Ted who repaired bicycles out of his garage, mentioned that his nephew's roommate at the college Emile was attending in the fall was in the physics program, the exact program Emile had chosen, and gave Emile the nephew's number without anyone asking.

He didn't call the number. He carried it around in his pocket for three days, on a receipt folded twice, and he wasn't sure why. Maybe because using it felt like admitting that Danny and Priya were replaceable, which they weren't, or maybe because the whole idea, that the edges of your life mattered as much as the center, still felt like a betrayal of the year he had just had, the best year, the year of Priya's basement and Danny's terrible car and the night they walked to the reservoir. It was possible, he thought, that both things were true at once and that no principle reconciled them. The strong ties carried you; the weak ones opened doors you didn't know were doors. He could hold both. He could also be wrong.

The morning his mother came back with the last box, she found him on the porch reading Granovetter's actual paper, which he had ordered used, and she asked what it was. "A guy in 1973," Emile said, "figured out people get jobs through people they barely know." She nodded slowly, the way she nodded at things she suspected were more than they sounded.

On Saturday Danny called again, the reception better this time, and told a long story about the party, and Emile laughed in the right places, sitting on the floor of a house that was starting to smell like food and cardboard and, faintly, like them. Afterward he took the receipt out of his pocket and unfolded it on his knee, the nephew's number creased into four pale squares, and dialed.

Antoine's grandmother had led the Seder for as long as anyone could remember, and this year, in February, she had handed him the Haggadah at the end of a long Sunday lunch and said only, "Your turn." He had carried the book home on the train like something that might bruise. It was a paperback, its spine cracked to whiteness, its pages soft with decades of thumbing, and when he opened it that night he felt the peculiar weight of a text that was not his to change but was now his to carry.

He spent two weeks preparing. He read the whole thing aloud in his room, twice, timing himself, marking where the Hebrew was transliterated for people like him who could sound out the letters but not slow down enough to mean them. He made a chart of the Seder's fifteen steps on a legal pad, and he practiced the blessings into his phone and played them back, wincing at his own flat delivery. His roommate Theo, who was not Jewish and had never denigrated anything in his life except cafeteria pasta, listened through the wall one night and came in to say it actually sounded kind of beautiful.

The gathering was at his uncle Daniel's house, twenty-three people, three tables pushed together in an L, the good chairs borrowed from the synagogue. Antoine arrived early with the brisket his father had made, and found his grandmother already seated near the head, smaller than he remembered, her hands folded on the tablecloth as though she had been waiting a long time. "You'll do fine," she said, which was not the same as saying it would be fine, and he understood the difference.

The trouble began almost immediately, and it was not the trouble he had rehearsed for. His cousin Maya, who was nine and had decided this year that she was too old to be given only the easy parts, had taken possession of the stack of extra Haggadot and was flipping through them with the concentration of a lawyer preparing a case. "I want the long one," she announced. "The one Tante reads. The part about the exodus, when they get out of Egypt."

"The whole point is that everyone gets a turn," her father said, a pugnacious note creeping in, as it did whenever Maya dug in her heels. "You can't just take the good parts."

But Maya had found something true, Antoine realized, listening to them argue over the spinach dip. The Haggadah retold the story of the Israelites leaving slavery in Egypt, but it did so in pieces, scattered through blessings and songs and questions, and whoever handed out the passages decided what the evening would feel like. Maya was not being greedy. She was asking how the story got told, and by whom, and whether a nine-year-old could hold the part where the sea split.

He made a decision that was not on his legal pad. Instead of assigning the readings the way his grandmother always had, oldest to youngest down the table, he went around the room and asked each person which passage they wanted, and then, where the requests collided, he split the long sections at the seams. Maya got the exodus narrative itself, all of it, because she asked first and asked hardest. His grandfather, who mumbled, got a short blessing. Uncle Daniel wanted nothing and was given, over his objection, the Four Questions, which he hadn't read since 1981 and delivered in a monotone that made the little kids laugh.

Somewhere in the middle of the meal, between the matzah ball soup and the main course, Antoine looked up from leading the Four Sons and saw his grandmother watching him with an expression he could not parse. Later, when everyone had moved to the living room and the Afikoman had been ransomed back from the cousins who had hidden it, she beckoned him into the kitchen. "You changed the order," she said.

"I did." He waited, ready to defend it, ready also to apologize.

"I want you to know I noticed," she said, and then, after a pause that lasted through the clatter of someone stacking dishes, "and that I didn't stop you." She took his wrist, briefly, the way she did, and went back toward the noise of the family, and Antoine stayed by the sink understanding that she had handed him the Seder the way you hand over anything that matters, which is to say without instructions, and that next year he would do some of it differently and not know until afterward which parts those were.

He was still standing there when Maya appeared in the doorway with her coat half on. "Next year," she said, "can we do the plagues outside? With the water?"

Aaron had read the message eleven times before he answered it. Maya said she liked old diners and bad coffee, so he suggested the Starlight on Route 9, which had both, and she sent back a single thumbs-up that he spent forty minutes interpreting.

He got to the diner nine minutes early, which he knew was a mistake as soon as he sat down. Nine minutes gave him time to think. He rearranged the sugar packets, put them back, and took out his phone, not to text anyone but to hold something. His father passed through the kitchen doorway behind the counter, saw him, and raised an eyebrow. Aaron's family had owned the Starlight for two generations, a lineage his father mentioned whenever anyone asked where Aaron worked, and tonight Aaron had not told Maya any of it. He had said he knew the place. That was technically true and also a kind of lie, and he sat with that while the booth vinyl squeaked under him.

She came in at six exactly, jeans and a college sweatshirt even though she was a senior like him, and she said, "You beat me here," and he said, "Only just," which was a lie too, and smaller.

They ordered. She asked about his summer and he told her about the community college physics course he'd taken, the one real ambitious thing he'd done, and he could hear himself making it sound bigger than it was. He talked about the professor's demonstrations, a thing with a pendulum, and she listened with her chin on her hand. When he ran out of demonstrations he asked about her, and she said she'd been rejected from her first-choice school in March and had decided not to be bitter about it, and the way she said it made him think she was still deciding.

The coffee arrived. Aaron reached for his cup at the same moment Maya shifted her elbow, and the cup went over, a brown sheet across the table, coffee running into the saucer and the napkin dispenser and the edge of her sweatshirt's sleeve.

"I'm so sorry," he said. He was up with paper napkins before she'd moved. "That's, wow, that's exactly how I wanted this to go."

"It's fine," she said, dabging at her sleeve. "It's old."

"I've ruined your shirt. I've ruined the table. My dad owns this place and now I've ruined the table."

She laughed then, a short surprised sound, and he realized he'd told her the thing he'd decided not to tell her, and that it had landed better than anything he'd rehearsed. He kept wiping. His father drifted over with a rag, said nothing, gave Maya a nod, and drifted away. Aaron sat back down with a wet handful of napkins and no cup.

"Here's a thing," Maya said. "In 1966, this psychologist, Elliot Aronson, ran an experiment. There's a quiz contestant who comes off as really competent, and then the contestant spills a cup of coffee. Afterward people rated the contestant more likable. It's called the pratfall effect." She shrugged. "Screwing up in front of someone can actually help. My sister studies psych."

"So you're saying I did that on purpose."

"I'm saying you have terrible aim."

He wanted to say that he didn't believe her, that people malign psychology findings to make themselves feel better about small disasters, that a study from 1966 with one contestant couldn't stand for every spilled cup in every diner. But he also wanted to believe her, because the evening had changed when the coffee went over. Before it he had been performing a version of himself, competent Aaron, physics-course Aaron, and the performance was rigid and he could feel it straining. After it he was just a guy with wet napkins, and that guy was easier to be, more ductile, bending where the other one would have snapped.

"Maybe," he said. "Or maybe it only works for the competent person. Maybe if I hadn't spent ten minutes talking about that physics course, you'd just think I'm clumsy and boring."

"You did spend ten minutes on the physics course."

"I know."

"It was kind of sweet," she said. "The pendulum thing."

His father brought two fresh cups without being asked and set them down far from Aaron's elbow, on Maya's side. He gave Aaron a look that Aaron could not read at all, or could read in two opposite ways. Aaron put his hands in his lap and let Maya take hers first.

They stayed until the pie case went dark at eight. Outside, under the buzzing sign, she said, "This was better than the coffee deserved," and he couldn't tell if that meant there would be another one, and he decided, while unlocking his bike, that not knowing was tolerable. She was still standing there when he looked back.

"Text me when you're home," she said.

The arena smelled like burnt pretzels and cold rubber, and Audrey had claimed the end of the row so she could see the whole ice instead of just the corner where her little brother kept pointing. The championship game had forty seconds left in the third period and her uncle's college team was up by one, and everyone around her, her mother, her uncle Dale, her cousin Priya, and Priya's friend Marcus, was leaning forward as though proximity could help.

Marcus was the loudest. He had never set foot on ice in his life; he'd come because Priya came, and he'd spent the first period asking what icing meant and the second period shouting coaching advice he clearly invented. Now he gripped the rail in front of them, knuckles pale, and when the goalie smothered a rebound with eleven seconds left, Marcus screamed, "Come on, we got this, we got this."

Audrey heard it and felt something snag in her mind, the way a sleeve catches on a nail. We. He said we. She had read something about that, late one night in October, in her psychology textbook's chapter on social identity, and she hadn't thought about it since. The clock hit zero, the crowd surged, and Marcus threw his arms around Priya and shouted, "We won! We won!" while her uncle wept openly into his scarf.

Outside, in the slush of the parking lot, everyone rehashed the game. Marcus narrated the final penalty kill as though he'd been on the bench for it, and Audrey watched him, feeling uncharitable and curious at once. "You said 'we' the whole third period," she said, not quite a question. "You've never even skated."

"It's the team," Marcus said. "It's, like, our school kind of. My cousin went there." He said it cheerfully, unembarrassed, and Priya laughed, and Audrey's mother told her not to interrogate guests. But it wasn't interrogation. She genuinely wanted to know why the word had bothered her when it clearly bothered her, when the truth was she'd said "we" too, once, in the second period, and then caught herself and switched to "they scored," and she couldn't say why the switch had felt like honesty rather than distance.

That night she found her textbook in the stack by her bed, its spine cracked from the fall semester, and turned back to the pages she'd half-read at midnight. There it was, in a paragraph about group identity: a 1976 study by a researcher named Robert Cialdini. After the university football team won, students wore more of the school's clothing. And when students described the games, they said "we" more when talking about wins than about losses. She read it twice. The words on the page had a provenance she could trace, a citation, a year, a method, and they described exactly what she'd watched happen in section twelve, row F, with the pretzel smell and the screaming.

She sat with it for a while, her desk lamp making a small bright territory in the dark room. Part of her wanted to text Marcus immediately, to hold the finding up like evidence at a trial, because there was a pleasure in catching someone in something. But that pleasure felt thin, almost evanescent, there and gone as soon as she noticed it. The study wasn't about Marcus being a fraud. Marcus knew he hadn't played. Everyone knew. He said "we" anyway, openly, joyfully, and nobody was deceived, least of all himself. The study was about something larger and stranger, about how a win could seep into people and make them claim a connection that a loss would leave them quietly dropping, like a hand letting go of a rail.

The next morning her uncle was still floating. He wore the team hoodie to breakfast, which he had not worn to the game, which Audrey noticed and did not say was significant, because she was watching herself now too. Over pancakes he asked what she'd thought of the ending, and she said, carefully, "Did you notice people say 'we won' but they say 'they lost'?" Her uncle frowned, half annoyed, half amused. "We had a bad period in the second," he said. "Anybody could see that." Then he went back to his coffee, and Audrey held her fork very still, because he had just done it, right there, the switch, without hearing it at all. She had done it too, last night, and the knowing didn't make her immune; that was the part she couldn't resolve.

She had two ideas in her that didn't fit together neatly, and she was honest enough with herself to admit it. One idea said the "we" was a kind of theft, secondhand glory, borrowing an achievement whose provenance was other people's years of 5 a.m. practices and stitched eyebrows and taped wrists. The other idea said that belonging was the whole point of sitting in a cold arena with your family, that the "we" was less a claim than an offering, a way of saying I'm attached to this, I'm part of the joy. The study suggested people did it without deciding to, more after wins than losses, which made it less a lie than a tide. But a tide was still not the same as a choice, and Audrey couldn't decide whether she wanted it to be.

By Monday the arena was empty again, the rink back to its public skating schedule, and Audrey went after school because Priya wanted to practice and Audrey owned skates and a vague competence. The ice was scarred and resurfaced, scarred again, its perfection from Saturday already gone, as evasive as Saturday itself. Marcus came too, wobbled along the boards, and fell twice, laughing, his palms red from the cold. When he got up the second time he said, "Okay, when I do this in college, we're going all the way." Audrey glided backward a few feet, considering him, considering her own mouth, which had almost said we.

"You could say 'I'll go all the way,'" she said. "It's your skating."

Marcus considered this with more seriousness than she expected, breath steaming, hair stuck to his forehead. "But it's better with a we," he said. Then he pushed off from the boards, arms out like a scarecrow, and Priya caught his sleeve and pulled him along, and Audrey followed, all three of them slow and unsteady and picking up speed toward the far circle.

Faith arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided to treat as a character flaw rather than a virtue, and took the stool at the window counter of the creamery with the best view of the door. The shop smelled of waffle cones and scorched sugar. Behind the glass, a teenager on summer furlough from some college scooped pistachio with the reluctance of someone who had already enervated himself with the heat, dragging the scoop in slow, defeated circles. Faith ordered a small maple walnut because it seemed like an epicurean choice, the kind of thing a person with developed taste would pick, and then regretted it because she did not actually like maple walnut that much.

Caleb was due at four. They had met at the used bookstore where she worked Saturdays, where he had spent forty minutes in the philosophy section and finally bought a paperback about the history of experiments, apologizing twice for taking so long. She had liked the apologizing. She had liked even more that he read the acknowledgments standing at the register before he paid, as though the book were a letter addressed to him.

He came in at 4:03, hair flattened on one side from a helmet, because he had biked. He had told her he would bike, and he had. That was already more reliability than certain people she could name. He sat down across from her and put the paperback on the counter between them like a passport.

"Did you finish it?" she asked.

"Almost. There's this one study I keep thinking about." He turned the cone the girl brought him, vanilla with sprinkles, as if rotating it might help him decide where to start. "In 1974 these two researchers, Dutton and Aron, had a woman interview men on a bridge. Some of the men had just crossed this frightening suspension bridge, the wobbly kind over a gorge. The others crossed a sturdy bridge, a normal one. The men who'd just crossed the frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call her afterward."

"Call the interviewer?"

"That's the whole thing. More of them called."

Faith licked her maple walnut and thought about it. "So a scary bridge makes you think you like somebody."

"Or makes something happen that they mistook for liking. That's the part I can't stop chewing on." He looked genuinely bothered, which she found more interesting than the study. "The book doesn't say why. It just says they called."

Outside, a man was parallel parking a sedan with great patience and no success, pulling forward, adjusting, easing back. The window put a hot stripe of light across the counter between their cones. Faith watched the car and tried to locate her own pulse, which was doing something steady and unremarkable, and she was not sure whether to be relieved or insulted.

"Okay," she said, "so here's my problem. I was nervous all morning. Like, stomach-flip nervous. And I couldn't tell if that meant I liked you, or if I was just scared of the date itself. Two separate things, same feeling."

Caleb set down his cone. "That's exactly the bridge thing."

"It's the opposite of the bridge thing. Those men didn't know they were on anything. I knew. I'm standing on the sturdy bridge, and I'm scared anyway." She had not planned to say that much. The maple walnut was not improving with exposure, and she kept eating it out of stubbornness.

"Maybe you're on both bridges," he said. "Maybe you like me and you're scared of the date, and you'd still be calling the interviewer either way."

"But the study doesn't cover that."

"No. The study just covers who called." He smiled, briefly, at his own cone. "I like that you're arguing with a study from 1974."

The scooper, wiping the counter with a rag, drifted past and turned the thermostat down a notch, and the compressor's hum changed key. Faith thought about her mother, who believed you should never trust a feeling you couldn't explain, and her sister, who believed you should never explain a feeling you could simply have. She had spent most of her life trying to decide between them, and here, with melting ice cream and a boy who read acknowledgments, she arrived somewhere in the middle: the pounding heart was ambiguous, this was true, but you could still choose what to do next, and the choosing was its own kind of evidence. What she could not yet say was what the choice would be. That part stayed open, like a door she could see light through.

She pushed the maple walnut aside, unfinished, an honest surrender.

"I'm not going to know today," she said. "I just want to say that out loud so I stop pretending."

"Understood." Caleb tore a napkin into two halves and offered her one, though she hadn't spilled anything. "For whenever you need it."

They sat with that for a minute. Outside, the man finally parked, climbed out, and stood looking at his car and then at the gap it had left from the curb, weighing some private question of good enough.

"Do you want to walk somewhere?" Caleb asked. "There's a footbridge over the canal. It's the sturdy kind."

Faith took the napkin anyway and put it in her pocket. "Show me."

The folder sat open on the kitchen table when Brandon came downstairs, and inside it was a contract with his mother's signature on the last page, dated yesterday. The first page said VACATION CLUB MEMBERSHIP AGREEMENT in gold letters, and under that, in a font so small he had to squint, the words terms and conditions appeared four times before the second paragraph. His mother was at the sink, not washing anything, just holding a sponge.

"Some man at the hotel," she said. "There was a booth in the lobby. He said it was a one-day rate." She had gone to her high school reunion, and on the way out, between the banquet room and the parking garage, a man in a navy blazer had folded her into a chair and slid papers across a folding table. Nineteen hundred dollars. She had signed where the arrows pointed, initialed where the little tabs said Buyer Initials, and driven home exhilarated, she admitted, by the idea that she had done something spontaneous for once in her life.

Brandon took the folder to his room and set it beside his keyboard. He was eighteen and had signed exactly one thing in his life, a student loan entrance counseling form, and he had read every line of it twice because the words liability and default had a weight to them, like stones in a river. His mother had not read anything. He opened the contract and found the section headed CANCELLATION, which said the buyer waived all rights to cancel after accepting the introductory bonus, whatever that was. A gift bag, she'd told him. A beach towel and a cooler.

He typed can you cancel a contract signed at a hotel booth into the search bar, and the results came back so fast it felt like the machine had been waiting for the question. The Federal Trade Commission, a page with the plain look of official antiquity, pale blue headings and no advertisements, described something called the Cooling-Off Rule. Buyers could cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations, the page said, until midnight of the third business day after the sale. He read the sentence three times. A hotel lobby booth, he was fairly sure, counted as a temporary location. It had been a folding table. The man had carried his brochures in a rolling suitcase.

"Mom," he called down the stairs, "when did you sign it?" Saturday. Today was Monday. He counted on his fingers, then counted again, because business days, he suspected, did not include Sunday, and he did not want to be wrong about the arithmetic of getting her money back. Tuesday, Wednesday, midnight Wednesday. He looked at the clock: 4:40 in the afternoon, and the days ahead of him suddenly felt glacial, each hour between now and that deadline moving slower than any hour of summer ever had.

The contract itself turned out to have a Notice of Cancellation form stapled inside the back cover, two copies, with lines for a date and a signature. The salesman was required to have told her about it, his mother said; he had mentioned something about paperwork while pointing at the signature line, and she had nodded, which she now understood was not the same as consent to anything except being nodded at. Brandon filled out one copy in his own careful handwriting, printing her name where it said the buyer, and then stopped, because the form asked for a signature and the signature was hers.

He brought it downstairs. She dried her hands and read it, all of it, which took a while, and Brandon watched her face do something complicated, embarrassment folding into stubbornness folding into relief. "I was so sure I'd missed my window," she said. "He made it sound like the moment I picked up the pen, it was done."

"That's kind of the whole trick," Brandon said. "The signature makes you feel like it's finished. But the rule gives you the third business day. Midnight." He slid the pen across the table to her. She signed the notice, and then he addressed an envelope to the vacation club's office, which was listed in the terms, in a strip mall two towns over, and wrote the words Cooling-Off Rule on a sticky note and pressed it to the front, in case anyone at the other end needed reminding what the paper was.

They drove to the post office together before it closed and asked the clerk at the counter for a stamped receipt, which the FTC page had suggested, and Brandon held the little slip of paper up to the window light as they walked back to the car, wondering whether the man in the navy blazer kept a tally of the envelopes that came back, and whether he ever wondered, on his slow nights, how many of his buyers had gone home and found a son at a computer.

Ashley had spent the first week of camp avoiding the art shack, because the art shack was where everyone went to make lanyards and glazed turtles, and she wanted to make something real. But on Tuesday the printmaking table was empty, the inks were actually dry, and the paper was heavy and toothy, so she sat down and started a landscape of the lake from memory. She had been drawing the same lake all summer in her notebook: water, hills, the strip of land that joined the camp's island to the shore like an isthmus in miniature, though she had never called it that until a boy in her cabin pointed at it and used the word, and it stuck.

Priya from the neighboring cabin leaned over her shoulder and said, "Move the waterline. Put the horizon a third of the way down."

"Why a third?"

"Because that's where horizons go. Rule of thirds."

"Who made that a rule?" Ashley asked. Priya had no answer, only a shrug, and the shrug bothered Ashley more than the advice did. She had come to camp with two ideas in her head that she could not get to sit together: that making art meant following what worked, and that following what worked was a small kind of dying. She did not say this out loud. She said, "It looks fine the way it is," and kept the horizon dead center, and Priya wandered off to the glazing kiln.

The print came out wrong. Not bad exactly, but inert, the lake sitting in the picture like a specimen pinned under glass, everything symmetrical and nothing alive. Ashley held it up to the light and hated it with the specific hatred reserved for your own careful work. Her counselor had told her on the first night that camp was for trying things, which Ashley had found obdurate and useless as advice, the kind of thing adults said instead of anything. But she thought of it now anyway.

The art shack had one shelf of books, warped by humidity, and she went through them on Wednesday afternoon while a group of eleven-year-olds slapped paint onto birdhouses. In a faded volume on composition she found the sentence, and she read it twice, and then a third time with her finger under the words. The phrase rule of thirds had been written down first by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery. She carried the book to Priya at the picnic table outside and set it down between their sandwiches.

"Some guy named John Thomas Smith," Ashley said. "1797. Remarks on Rural Scenery. He's the first one who wrote the phrase down."

"See," Priya said. "It's a real rule."

"That's not what it says." Ashley was surprised by her own certainty. "It says one guy wrote it down in 1797. It doesn't say he was right, or that it was always true, or that it has to be true for me." But even as she said it, she was looking at the lake, at the actual lake, where the far shore sat low against the water and the sky took everything above it, and she could see that the world itself did not halve neatly. The horizon out there was already sitting somewhere below the middle. Smith had noticed something, she thought; he had not invented it, he had caught it.

So on Thursday she cut a new block, and this time she set the waterline a third of the way down, but she kept the isthmus off-center to the left, running against the grain of every suggestion Priya had made, and she pushed the hills until they crowded the top of the frame, unresolved, unfinished. The print that came off the press was better. Not good. Better. It had a nervous energy to it, the land pressing down on the water, and when Priya saw it she stood quiet for a second and said, "I like it better off-center. The isthmus, especially. I was wrong about that part."

"You were right about the other part," Ashley said. "That's the annoying thing."

She pinned both prints to the corkboard by the shack door, the symmetric one and the new one, side by side, so that anyone walking past would have to decide which they liked without being told. Priya wrote under the first one, in pencil, SMITH, 1797, and under the second one she wrote nothing, and Ashley understood that too, because some things you cannot instantiate in a caption. She stood in front of them until the mosquitoes drove her inside, and through the screen door she could still see the lake past both horizons, the real one, doing whatever it wanted.

Isaac had planned to finish his demographics project at home, but his mother's conference had swallowed the apartment for the weekend, so he'd exiled himself to the food court with his laptop, a cold slice of pizza, and a printed stack of population pyramids that he now had to exhume from the bottom of his backpack, where they had fossilized under gym clothes. The assignment was due Monday: choose a country, read its pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Isaac had picked Qatar almost at random, because it was small and he liked the shape of its name.

The chart did not look like a pyramid. It looked like a wasp: a narrow head of children, a swollen striped middle, and almost nothing at the top. He stared at it, then turned the paper sideways, then held it up to the skylight as though the truth might come through from behind. The middle bulge was enormous, and it was lopsided in a way no pyramid had a right to be.

"That's a printing error," he said to nobody.

"There's no printer in the world that makes only men," said Priya, sliding into the seat across from him with her own tray. She was in his geography class and had the suspicious good cheer of someone whose project was already done. "What is that, a bee?"

"It's Qatar. It's supposed to be a population pyramid." He pointed at the long bars on the left side of the bulge, the side his textbook's legend said was male. The female bars beside them were less than half as long. "Unless Qatari women have been secretly leaving the country in huge numbers, this chart is broken. I'm going to fail. Mr. Okafor will frame my failure in the staff room."

Priya leaned in, chewing thoughtfully. "Maybe it's not broken. Maybe it's real and it's just weird."

"Charts aren't weird. Charts are honest. That's the whole point of charts." Isaac said this with the conviction of a boy who had, until this moment, never deeply trusted anything else. He turned the paper over. Blank. He turned it back. Still a wasp.

He did what any seventeen-year-old researcher does: he pulled out his phone and typed Qatar population pyramid male bulge, half expecting to find a forum full of people complaining about a bad dataset. What he found instead stopped his thumb mid-scroll. The bulge was real. Some Gulf states, Qatar among them, showed a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers lived there. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt the ground of the assignment shift slightly under him, like a ferry leaving the dock while you're still looking at your ticket.

"Okay," he said slowly. "So the chart isn't lying. The men are there. They're just, a lot of them, not from there." He spread his hands over the wasp's midsection as though warming them at a fire. "So if I'm predicting schools or nursing homes, what do I even do with them? They're in the pyramid but they're not really in the, the population. Or they are in the population. Argh."

"That sounds like a you problem," said Priya, stealing a pepperoni. "Also a Qatar problem, honestly."

"It's both problems. That's the problem." Isaac began scribbling in the margin. The children at the top of the chart, the narrow head, were the school question; the near-empty peak was the nursing home question, or the lack of one. But the bulge, that striped middle full of working-age men, didn't fit either prediction cleanly, and he couldn't decide whether to count it, average it out, or flag it and move on. His notes said all three, in that order, and then a small drawing of a wasp wearing a hard hat.

Priya peered at the notes. "Wow. Demographic acumen. You should put that on a business card."

"You don't know what acumen means."

"Neither do you, obviously, or you'd have an answer."

Mr. Okafor, when Monday came, walked the rows with his hands behind his back and paused at Isaac's desk longer than at anyone else's. He looked at the pyramid, at the margin notes, at the wasp in the hard hat, and at the final paragraph, which ended with a question mark Isaac had written in pen and then, unable to help himself, circled.

"So," said Mr. Okafor. "Schools or nursing homes?"

"That depends who you count," said Isaac. "Which depends on who you think the pyramid is for. I have an answer for the citizens and a different answer for everybody in the chart, and I don't know which one you want, and I'm not sure I think there's a right one. Also I think my brain is igneous, it cooled under pressure and now it's stuck like this."

"That's geology," said Mr. Okafor.

"It's also my weekend."

Mr. Okafor smiled and moved on without marking anything, and Isaac looked down at his circled question mark, and then at the wasp, and then out the window, where the flagpole rope was tapping in the wind.

"Mr. Okafor," he called after him. "Seriously. Which one would you build?"

"I'd build a canteen," said Mr. Okafor, without turning around, "for all those working-age men."

The October light through the gym's high windows turned the floor a dull gold, and beyond the chain-link fence outside, the arboreal edge of the park had already gone rust and yellow. Lucas stood at the baseline with the rest of the junior varsity squad, waiting for Coach Reyes to finish writing on his clipboard, and tried not to look at Danny, who was two spots down the line and pretending to stretch a hamstring he had never once pulled.

The problem was simple and Lucas had been turning it over for two weeks: the team loafed. Not in games, exactly, but in practice, in the conditioning drills, in every moment when the sprint was collective and the shame could be spread thin across twelve bodies. When they ran lines as a group, the whole pack drifted to the pace of its slowest concealer. Lucas wanted playing time, and playing time went to the coach's eye, and the coach's eye, he suspected, could not tell who was actually working inside a crowd of identical jerseys.

"Sprint times today," Coach Reyes said, slapping the clipboard against his palm. "Individually. One at a time, everyone watching, everyone timed."

Danny groaned, loud enough to destabilize the loose attention of the line, and a couple of guys laughed, and the laugh was the old sound, the sound of the group absorbing a complaint so that no single person owned it. Lucas felt the laughter move past him like weather.

First up was Marcus, a center who usually drifted through conditioning like a man wading through shallow surf. Marcus ran the length of the floor four times, touched each baseline, and crossed the finish at a time Lucas would not have believed on Sunday. The clock said otherwise. Then Avery, then Razaan, then a sophomore whose name Lucas kept forgetting, all of them faster than they had been on Monday, some of them faster than they had been all season.

"Cooper," the coach called, and Danny jogged to the line.

Danny ran hard. Lucas watched him do it, watched the lazy joke of a boy push through four lengths at a time only two tenths slower than Lucas's own best, and understood something that had been sitting in the back of his mind since a unit in psych class he had half slept through. In groups, people put out less. He could not have said why, and he did not try. But when each runner's time went up on the whiteboard with a name beside it, the effort was different, and the difference was not small.

After practice, in the parking lot under the bare sycamores, Lucas caught Danny pulling his hoodie over his head. "You know what that was," Lucas said. "Back there."

"A timed sprint?"

"Social loafing," Lucas said. "People slack off in groups. Less when everyone can see who did what."

Danny zipped his bag with a slow, deliberate tug. "So you're saying I'm a loafer."

"I'm saying we all were. Me too. Monday I hid in the pack same as anybody." Lucas heard how it sounded, the confession arriving too neatly, and let it sit there ungilded. "I wanted the times posted before I even knew what it was called. I told Coach the scoreboard wasn't enough for conditioning."

"You asked him?"

"Tuesday."

Danny looked at him for a long moment, and under the look was the whole season: the two of them competing for the same starting spot, the months of Danny's jokes marking the border between them, and now this, the fact that Lucas had quietly rearranged the rules of the world they both lived in. "So now everybody has to sprint their ass off every practice," Danny said. "Because you wanted an edge."

"Because I wanted it to mean something when I beat you out," Lucas said. "If you loaf and I don't, I never know if I was better. Now we both go all the time, and whoever wins the spot wins it for real."

The honesty landed wrong at first, or right in a way that stung; Danny shouldered his bag and walked three steps toward the lot before stopping. The wind moved through the trees above them, scattering a few leaves across the asphalt. "It's like the group kind of falls apart on its own," Danny said, not turning around. "Like entropy or something. Unless somebody's keeping score."

"Something like that," Lucas said. He was not sure it was true, was not sure the analogy held, was not sure whether wanting a fair fight made him honorable or just made him someone who had found a more elaborate way to win. The uncertainty did not feel like weakness. It felt like standing at the free-throw line knowing the shot could go either way.

"Fine," Danny said, turning back. "Tuesday, then. You and me, first two names on the board. Loser carries the balls all week."

"Losers carry the balls," Lucas said. "That's what managers are for."

"That's what you're for if you lose." Danny grinned, and it was almost the old grin, altered by something Lucas could not yet name.

Tuesday morning the gym was cold and the whiteboard was blank and clean, and Lucas stepped to the baseline first, sneakers squeaking against the gold-lit floor.

Alexandre's first shift at Ferreira's Market began with a tour that lasted four minutes, most of it spent on the time clock. Manny, the floor manager, showed him the dairy cooler, the loading dock, and the pallet jack he was not yet licensed to drive, then handed him a box cutter and walked away. The rest Alexandre learned by inference: the schedule taped behind the register, the laminated card in his onboarding folder that said he would earn minimum wage for ninety days, and the small blue placard by the break room sink that read, in calm letters, that this store was represented by Local 304 and that his rights under the collective agreement were posted on the board beside the schedule.

He spent the afternoon stocking canned tomatoes. A woman named Dot, who had worked the aisles for eleven years, stopped her cart beside him and watched him arrange the tins label-forward. "You're putting the store brand at eye level," she said. "Contract says house brands go on the bottom shelf. Management complains every year and every year we keep the clause. Small thing, but it was traded for something once, so we keep it." She said this the way people describe weather, and rolled on toward aisle six.

On his break he wandered to the back of the store, past the walk-in freezer, looking for the bathroom he had not yet found. Instead he found a door marked FIRE EXIT, and in front of it, a wall of cardboard boxes stacked almost to the ceiling, some of them split and leaking a smell of detergent. He stood there a moment. In eleventh grade, Mr. Okoye had spent a whole period on the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York, March 25, 1911, and Alexandre had written it on a test and forgotten it. Now it came back with the smell of that classroom, the radiator, the photocopy of a photograph. One hundred forty-six garment workers had died, many of them trapped because the exit doors had been locked. He remembered being sixteen and thinking the number was ancient history, the kind of thing that happened before people knew better.

He moved two boxes. The wall did not visibly shrink. He looked at the door handle, at the boxes, at the ceiling sprinkler that had a cobweb on it like a small flag of surrender.
