She had wanted an answer for two years, had postulated since freshman year that an acceptance would settle everything, that the moment the email came, the anxious machinery in her chest would finally stop.

The machinery had not stopped. It had, if anything, found new work.

She typed a sentence about Northwestern's journalism program and deleted it. The radiator clanked. Someone near the front was eating an orange, and the citrus smell cut through the stuffy heat, sharp and specific, and she thought suddenly of her mother peeling oranges on the porch last summer, saying, you'll go where you go, it doesn't matter to me, which Alexa had understood even then to be a kind of lie, a generous one. Her mother wanted the big school, the famous one, the one whose name made people at church nod. The school that had accepted her was good but not famous. The school she had 212 words about was both.

Priya slid into the seat beside her, having abandoned her own term paper. "You're still writing it," she said, almost accusing. "I can't believe you're still writing it."

"I don't know what I'm doing," Alexa said. "That's the honest answer. I have one yes in my hand and I don't know if it's the right yes, and if I stop now, I'll never find out what the other answers would have been."

"So apply everywhere. Keep all the doors open. What's the problem?"

"The problem is I've been beguiling myself for two years that one letter would make the decision for me. It doesn't. It just moves the decision to December instead of April."

Priya was quiet for a moment, chewing on this. "That's still a better problem than Derek's."

Alexa glanced at Derek, at the rejection letter now folded into a small square on his desk, at his hood, at the window behind him where the fog was thick enough to draw in. She picked up her finger and drew a letter A, then wiped it away with her sleeve, because it felt like claiming something she hadn't claimed yet.

"What's the essay about?" Priya asked.

"Supposedly, why I want to go there."

"And why do you?"

Alexa looked at the 212 words on her screen. They were true words, careful words, and they had nothing in them she could point to and call a reason. She set her hands on the keyboard. "Give me until the deadline," she said. "Twelve days. Then I'll tell you both of us."

Mr. Delgado rapped his knuckles on his desk and announced twenty minutes left in the period, and the orange smell reached the back row, and Alexa began to type.

The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Ava stood at the register of Korner Supply on a Tuesday morning in June, filling out the last form between her and an apron. She had already written her name twice, once in her careful hand and once in her rushing hand, and both looked like they belonged to someone younger. The form was called a W-4, the manager had said, sliding it across the counter with a pen that had a chewed cap, and now she was staring at a box that wanted to know something she did not understand at all.

"It tells me how much to withhold," she said slowly, reading the top line to herself. The words were English, each one individually familiar, but the sentence had the texture of a riddle. She gathered that the federal income tax was involved, and that each paycheck was involved, and that her answers would somehow connect the two, but the connecting logic was not on the page. Her mother would know. Her mother did the family taxes every April with a shoebox of receipts and a specific facial expression that Ava had learned not to interrupt.

She took out her phone and typed, "At the job. They gave me a form. W-4? Do you know what this is." Then she reconsidered the question mark, kept it anyway, and sent it. The manager, a broad man named Dale who wore his reading glasses on a cord around his neck, was unpacking a box of tape measures two aisles over, and she could hear him counting under his breath, forty-one, forty-two, as though the tape measures might disobey him.

Her phone buzzed. "Withholding. You fill out the W-4 so the employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck." Ava read the text twice. So the form was not a tax itself; it was a piece of information she handed over, and the store used it to do the taking-out. That felt manageable, almost polite, like telling someone in advance how you took your coffee. She filled in the lines her mother walked her through by text, one slow reply at a time, while a customer waited behind her to buy a single bolt.

"First job?" the customer asked. He was holding the bolt in his fist like evidence.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're apologizing to the pen," he said, and paid for his bolt and left.

Dale put her on paint for the first week, which suited her, because the paint aisle had a fan and because the names of the colors were their own small literature. There was a chip called Littoral Gray, a soft blue-green, and when a woman came in asking for something to remind her of the shore, Ava turned the fan deck to that one without having to look it up. "It's a coastal kind of color," she said, and the woman held it up to the light and said it was exactly the water at her grandmother's house in Maine, and bought two gallons.

The work had a substrate of repetition under everything else, she decided by Thursday: unlocking, sweeping, restocking, the register's little songs. But things kept surfacing through it. A man came in wanting to repaint his front door in a way that would, he admitted, "aggrandize the whole entryway," and Ava had not known that a door could be aggrandized, though she recognized the impulse, having spent a fair portion of her own energy on being perceived favorably. He chose a deep red. She mixed it on the shaker machine, which sounded like a small rebellion, and thought about how much of wanting to be seen was like paint, a coat you applied over whatever the door actually was.

The paycheck arrived on the fifteenth, in an envelope with her name typed on it, and it was smaller than the number she had computed in her head on the bus. She stood at the time clock doing the subtraction again, then looked at the stub, where a line item said FED INCOME TAX, and the riddle from her first morning assembled itself into sense. She had marked that box, and the store had done exactly what she told it to. It occurred to her that she had made a real decision, with consequences, at a moment when she felt entirely ignorant, and that the decision had worked anyway, more or less, the way most of her decisions seemed to. She could not decide whether that was reassuring or slightly frightening, and she suspected it was both, and that the two feelings were going to coexist for a while.

She texted her mother a photo of the stub. Her mother replied with a single thumbs-up, which Ava interpreted as pride filtered through whatever the parental equivalent of a W-4 was, some withholding of its own.

At closing, Dale asked how the first paycheck felt. Ava considered saying smaller than expected, or educational, or fine, and chose the truest available option.

"Like I told a form something and it listened," she said. Dale laughed once, a short bark, and handed her the keys to lock the paint aisle gate.

"You'll get faster at that bolt drawer," he said, and turned off the lights over the registers, one switch at a time, while the tape measures hung in their rows, waiting for morning.

The phone store smelled like new plastic and floor cleaner, and Emile stood at the counter holding his mother's old phone, the one with the crack running diagonally across the screen like a fault line on a map. His own phone had died three weeks ago, and he had a summer job starting Monday at the landscaping company, which meant he needed something that worked, today, before he had the money to pay for it outright.

The sales rep, a woman named Dana with a lanyard and the patient gravitas of someone who had explained the same forms a thousand times, turned a tablet toward him. "You can put it on a payment plan," she said. "Twenty-two a month for twenty-four months." Emile did the arithmetic in his head and felt something tighten. Twenty-two times twenty-four was five hundred twenty-eight. The phone's price tag said four hundred ninety-nine.

"So it costs more this way," he said. "Twenty-nine dollars more." Dana nodded without apology. "That's the interest," she said. "That's what borrowing costs. You're paying for the use of money you don't have yet." He looked at the tablet, at his own signature half-formed in the signature box, and thought about how the number was small enough to seem like nothing and large enough to be real.

Then Dana ran his information and paused. "There's a late payment here from March," she said. "Looks like a phone bill. It's showing on your credit." Emile's stomach dropped. He remembered it exactly: the app, the notification he'd swiped away during a chemistry study session, the bill that had slipped his mind for six weeks during track season. "How bad is that?" he asked. "Like, does one missed bill ruin everything?"

Dana turned the screen so he could see the breakdown. "Payment history is the largest factor in your FICO score," she said. "About thirty-five percent of it, for the general population." He read the numbers on the screen and understood, slowly, that the forgotten bill he had treated as nothing had touched the single biggest thing a lender would look at. Not all of it, not close, but the largest piece. "It fades," Dana added. "It's not forever. But it's there."

He signed, because Monday was coming and the job was real, and then he sat on the bench near the accessories wall while the transfer ran. Two college guys stood at the next counter, arguing in the easy, half-joking way of people who had read one article and become doctrinaire about it. "Credit's a trap," one said. "They design it to vilify the poor and forgive the rich." The other shook his head. "It's a tool. If you pay on time it works for you. My sister's score got her an apartment." They went back and forth, and Emile found himself unable to agree with either of them completely.

He thought about the twenty-nine dollars, about how the same force that took money from him when he borrowed could give money to him if he saved, because Dana had mentioned it offhand while ringing him up: his bank paid interest on savings, small but real, money earning money while he slept. Two directions of the same principle. He had missed a payment and that mistake would follow him, but it was thirty-five percent, not one hundred percent; the rest was still his to shape, starting with the twenty-two dollars due each month, which he now intended to automate so that neither track season nor chemistry nor anything else could swallow it again.

At home he set up the autopay and then, after a minute, moved forty dollars from checking into the savings account his mother had opened for him years ago and he had never touched. The interest rate was pitiful, something like one and a half percent, and he laughed a little at how little it would earn. Still, he watched the balance on the screen, four hundred and six dollars, and imagined it drifting upward while the phone debt drifted downward, two lines crossing somewhere in a future he couldn't quite see. His mother called from the kitchen asking if he wanted dinner. He closed the laptop and said, "Yeah, I'm coming."

Victor had spent three weeks drafting his bill on later school start times, and when the model parliament convened in the drafty assembly hall of the provincial legislature, he carried the typed pages like something living. The clerk, a university student named Priya in a borrowed black robe, called the house to order. Victor stood, his throat dry, ready to argue. "Bill 12, An Act to Amend the Education Act with Respect to School Start Times," Priya read, and before he could open his mouth she had moved on to the next item. Twelve seconds, maybe less. No questions, no debate, not even a vote. Around him the other students exchanged looks of pure bewilderment, and a girl named Marta whispered, "That was it? That was nothing."

At the lunch break Victor found Priya stacking the order paper and asked her whether his bill had been disqualified somehow, whether he had filled out a form wrong. She laughed, not unkindly. "That's first reading," she said. "In the real UK Parliament, a government bill's first reading is a formality. It just gets introduced, no debate, no vote." Victor stared at her, feeling oddly cheated. He had imagined the moment his idea entered the world as a public battle, not a name read into a record. "So it doesn't mean anything?" he asked. "It means it exists now," Priya said, and went back to her papers.

The committee stage came after lunch, and that was where the bleeding began. Victor had written a clause mandating a nine o'clock start for all high schools in the fictional province. A delegate from the rural party, a broad-shouldered boy named Ellis, moved an amendment allowing boards to opt out for bus scheduling reasons. Victor argued that an opt-out clause was a hole you could drive a bus through, and the room laughed, but the amendment carried anyway, eleven votes to nine. In the hallway afterward Ellis found him at the water fountain and offered something like an armistice: rural boards would accept the bill if they could breathe, and without rural boards, there would be no bill at all. Victor said he would think about it, which was true, and that it was a betrayal, which he also believed.

He thought about it through the debate that evening, sitting in the back benches while other bills rose and fell. A delegate proposing free menstrual products in schools watched her bill die at second reading on a voice vote, the "noes" rolling through the chamber like weather. Victor noticed that she did not cry, though her jaw worked. He noticed, too, that she was back at her desk within the hour, annotating a new draft in green ink. His friend Dev, slouched beside him, called this congenital optimism, the kind you were born with, and Victor envied it even as he distrusted it. Dev himself had come to the weekend to lose bills, he said, the way other people went to the gym.

What Victor worked out, slowly, in the yellow light of the chamber, was that two things he had been treating as one were actually two. He had wanted the law, and he had wanted to be right, and the committee had forced him to see that the second could cost him the first. He didn't think the trade was fair. He didn't think it was clean. But when debate on his own bill opened after dinner, he rose on a point of order and announced, to his own surprise, that he would accept the amendment as drafted. Marta, who had voted for the opt-out, looked at him strangely, almost disappointed, as though he had surrendered something she had wanted to watch him defend.

The third reading was almost quiet after that. Members who had fought him in committee now spoke of the bill as sensible, balanced, the kind of word that used to mean something before it meant nothing. The vote was called, and Victor watched the clerk tally the standing bodies in the aisles. Twenty-two for, seven against. A majority, an ordinary miracle, accomplished without anyone changing their mind about anything except him. Priya declared the bill passed, and the house moved on to the next order of business before his pulse had slowed.

The closing ceremony simulated royal assent. The Speaker, an actual retired MLA who had agreed to attend, sat beneath the carved provincial crest and read the titles of the bills that had survived the weekend, Victor's among them, in a flat ceremonial voice. "The bill receives assent and is now law," she said, and there was a small smattering of applause, mostly from parents who had drifted in for the last hour. Victor stood with the others while the Sergeant-at-Arms carried the mace out of the chamber, the old brass catching the light, the whole thing over.

Outside, in the parking lot, the evening had gone cold and the real buses were already idling. Ellis was loading a duffel bag into a minivan. "Your law's got a hole in it," he called across the asphalt. Victor shrugged into his jacket. "So does every law," he said. "I read the rest of the order paper." Ellis grinned and shut the van door, and Victor stood a moment longer listening to the engines.

The summer research slot came down to one afternoon in the optics lab, and Makayla had planned for it the way she planned for exams, which was to say too much and then sleep badly. Forty seniors from her school were rotating through the university's physics building in groups of six. Her group had drawn the spectroscopy bench on the third floor, where a graduate student named Corinne handed each of them a printed card and told them to record what they saw through the eyepiece.

Priya went first. She looked for a long time and wrote "faint dark lines, maybe three, hard to say." Then Corinne tapped the card and said, "For this demo, you're looking for bright emission lines in the green region. Four of them." Priya leaned back in, and within thirty seconds her pencil was moving. "Oh, yeah," she said. "Four. They're right there. I don't know how I missed it."

Makayla kept her eyes on the bench while the other four took their turns. Every one of them saw four lines after being told to expect four. When her turn came, she looked before Corinne said anything to her, and she saw what Priya had seen at first: dark lines, indistinct, count uncertain. She wrote that down. Corinne read it, then read it again.

"Interesting," Corinne said. "You're the only one who recorded dark lines."

"I wrote it before you told me what to look for," Makayla said. "Does that matter?"

Corinne didn't answer directly. She pulled a stool over and sat, which the other grad students in the room did not do. "Have you heard of René Blondlot?" she asked the group. Nobody had. "A French physicist, claimed to discover a new kind of radiation. He called them N-rays."

"Like X-rays," said Dario, the boy next to Makayla.

"Right. In 1904 another physicist, Robert W. Wood, went to Blondlot's lab and secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The observers still reported seeing the N-rays." Corinne stood up and straightened the eyepiece. "Wood didn't announce what he'd done until after. That's the part people remember."

Makayla turned her card over. On the back, in the margin, she had written her prep notes that morning, half of them definitions she'd exhumed from an old textbook in the school library, because the research program's application asked for a short essay on "how we know what we know." One of the notes said logos, from her English class, argument that persuades by reason. She had underlined it twice. Now the word looked thin to her, like it assumed reason was a thing one person could hold whole in one hand.

"Is this demo rigged, then?" Priya asked. There was an edge in her voice, and Makayla understood it. Priya had already emailed the program coordinator saying the lab visit confirmed her interest in optics.

"It's not rigged," Corinne said. "The lamp is exactly what I said it is. The question is what a single observer is worth."

Makayla thought about that on the walk to the next station, and she thought about it through the boring part of the tour, the clean room with its yellow light, and the part where Dario asked whether the university had ever retracted a paper. One result wasn't anything, she'd known that in an abstract way, but she hadn't felt it until Priya's pencil started moving. Still, she wasn't sure the feeling was fair. Priya wasn't lying. Corinne's tip about the green lines was presumably true, and Priya's second look was presumably better than her first. Expectation could point you at something real. The problem was that the pointing and the seeing felt identical from the inside, and only one of them counted as evidence.

At the bus turnaround she caught up with Corinne, who was carrying a crate of extension cords to a van. Makayla said she wanted to apply for the slot and asked, since it would come up in the essay, whether Corinne thought a study should be thrown out when the observers knew what they expected.

"One observer, one afternoon? That was never a study," Corinne said. She shifted the crate to her hip. "You'd repeat it, other people would repeat it with different instruments, people who wanted you to be wrong would repeat it. Then you'd know something."

"Unless they were all expecting the same thing," Makayla said.

"Then it takes longer," Corinne said. She loaded the crate and shut the van door.

On the bus Makayla wrote two sentences in her notebook and crossed out the second one, which had claimed too much. The first said that she had seen dark lines and had no way, from inside her own head, to certify them, and that the certification would have to come from outside her, repeatedly, from people with no stake in what she'd written. She looked at Priya two rows up, headphones in, filling out the program's online form on her phone. Priya typed fast, and stopped once, and looked out the window at the loading dock, and then typed again.

The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Nicholas had been rehearsing in the hallway long enough to notice both. He held his outline flat against a binder, the way he had seen lawyers do it in videos, and read the first line of his argument under his breath. In forty minutes he would stand before a panel of three judges in a borrowed courtroom and argue the student's side of Mahanoy Area School District v. B.L., the case his civics class had drawn by lottery. Then, after lunch, he would argue the school's side of the same case, which was the part nobody had warned him would be hard.

He had not chosen the case. Priya had pulled the slip from the coffee can and read the name aloud, and Marcus, who sat behind him, had laughed and said it sounded like a school board suing a letter. Nicholas had gone home that weekend and looked it up, partly for the assignment and partly because of something he had posted in March, a picture of his cross country coach with a caption he had deleted by Sunday but which three people had screenshotted. Nothing had come of it. Still, when he read the summary of the case, he felt the specific cold of recognition.

The case was about a girl who had posted something on Snapchat, off campus, on a weekend, and her school had punished her for it. Nicholas had assumed, before he read further, that the school was allowed to do that, that off campus was like a country the school's rules didn't reach but its arm did. Then he found the holding. In 2021, the Supreme Court had ruled 8 to 1 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Eight justices against one. He read the sentence twice, then copied it onto an index card, because it seemed like the kind of thing that shouldn't be paraphrased.

The courtroom was crepuscular in the late morning, the blinds tilted so that light fell in gray bars across the jury box, which sat empty. A bailiff who was actually a retired accountant let them in and told them not to touch the microphone. Nicholas took the petitioner's table, the one closest to the bench, and arranged his cards in order while Priya sat beside him with the case brief and a bag of pretzels she did not open. At the respondent's table, two juniors Nicholas didn't know well spread out their notes like a poker hand they were proud of.

"Ms. Reyes, you may begin whenever you're ready," said the judge in the center, a law student named Alanna who wore her father's old robe. Nicholas stood. His first two minutes went fine, better than fine; he talked about the post being made off campus, on her own time, and he said the line from his index card almost exactly, that the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 1 in 2021 that the school violated the student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Alanna nodded and wrote something down, and the nod coagulated all his scattered preparation into something that felt like actual confidence.

Then the judge on the left leaned forward. "Counsel, what would you say to the school if the post had disrupted a class on Monday?" It was the question Nicholas had hoped wouldn't come, because he had two answers and they disagreed with each other. He gave the student's answer first, that punishment for a weekend post stretches the school's reach into students' private lives. Then he stopped, because the honest thing was also true. "And I'd have to concede that schools aren't helpless," he said. "I just don't think the First Amendment turns off when a student walks through her front door."

At lunch, in the courthouse cafeteria, Marcus slid his tray across from Nicholas and asked how it had gone. "I don't know yet," Nicholas said. "Ask me after round two." The problem was the second round. For an hour he had believed the student's side so completely that he could feel it in his chest, and now he had to stand up and be the school, the district that had suspended a girl for swearing on a weekend. He spread his cards on the table and tried to see the other argument, but his thoughts kept sliding back, the way a whole biome shifts when one species is removed; the case without the student's rights in it wasn't the same case at all.

When the afternoon session began, the light had moved and the courtroom was warmer. Nicholas stood at the respondent's table and argued that a school could still act when off-campus speech bled into school life, that the majority had left the door open, that the lone dissenter had a point about schools needing to reach students wherever they were. He did not fully believe it, but he argued it carefully, and once, when Alanna asked whether a school should follow students home, he heard himself say, "Not home. But maybe the bus stop in between." It was the first thing all day that felt like his own.

The panel conferred, then awarded the round to the other side, and Priya squeezed his shoulder on the way out. In the hallway, the light through the high windows had gone amber, and Nicholas stopped by the water fountain and took a long drink. He still didn't know where the line was, exactly, between a school's reach and a student's life, and he suspected the Court didn't either, given eight votes on one side and a single stubborn voice on the other. He put his index cards back in order, both sets, one for each side, and slid them into his back pocket. "Same time next week," Priya said, holding the door.

The marble corridor outside Courtroom 4B smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Sophia's note cards kept slipping against her skirt. Fourteen students from three high schools had been assigned to litigate a mock case before a panel of real appellate judges, and Sophia had drawn the worst possible job: she would argue both sides. Petitioners in the morning, respondents after lunch, same girl, same bench, same fifteen minutes each.

The case was one her class had built from a real fight at a school two districts over. A student named in the file only as M.R. had posted a video mocking the vice principal, and the school had suspended her. That part was settled law, more or less. The twist her classmates had added was this: M.R. had also been banned from a private class-discussion website run by a company, and she claimed that ban violated her free speech rights too. Sophia had to argue that it did. Then, after lunch, she had to argue that it didn't.

In the morning she stood at the podium with her knees locked and said what she had prepared. She talked about the marketplace of ideas, about chilling expression, about a sixteen-year-old silenced in the very forum where her classmates gathered. Justice Kowalski, a heavyset man with reading glasses pushed low, leaned forward and asked whether the website was run by the government. Sophia said no, and he asked the question again, slower, the way you repeat something to someone who hasn't understood it the first time.

"Then walk me through it," he said. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. So what is your claim?"

Her argument dissolved in her mouth. She had known the words, of course, had copied them into her outline weeks ago, but she had never actually believed them until a judge made her stand there and look at them. She said something about students feeling that the platform was their town square, and the judge said feelings did not create jurisdiction, and a girl from the other school, a redhead named Priya who'd spent the whole morning smirking, whispered something to her co-counsel that Sophia pretended not to notice.

At lunch she sat alone on the courthouse steps and ate half a sandwich. Her grandmother had once been fired from a print shop for union organizing, and the family still argued about it at holidays, her uncle insisting it was illegal, her mother correcting him each time with visible exhaustion. Sophia had always assumed her mother was being pedantic. Now she understood her mother had been protecting the family from a confusion that would cost them something later, the way you teach a kid not to touch a stove. The government couldn't punish you for speaking. A private company could, mostly, and you had to know which one you were standing in front of.

But the afternoon side was not as easy as the morning side had been hard. Arguing that M.R.'s ban was lawful felt like handing a weapon to whoever owned the forum, and the forum was where everyone her age actually lived. She stood up after lunch and made the legal argument cleanly, almost coldly, and then Justice Alvarez, a small woman with silver hair, asked the counterpoint Sophia had been dreading: "Counsel, is there anything you find troubling about the rule you're defending?" Sophia paused, and then said yes, that the law drew a line between public power and private power at a moment when private platforms felt more like governments than governments did, and that the doctrine struck her as accurate and antiquated at once, which was not a distinction the First Amendment itself could resolve.

Justice Alvarez wrote something down. Priya, sitting in the second row, was not smirking anymore.

When the judges retired to score the round, Priya came over. "The morning," she said. "When you folded on the private website. You knew, right? I could tell you knew." Sophia admitted she had known and hoped the judges wouldn't press it, and Priya laughed, a real laugh, not a smirk. "I got that exact question wrong at a tournament in October. I claimed a platform violated a girl's free speech rights and a judge spent ten minutes dismantling me. I only challenged you today to see if you'd do the same thing I did."

They were still on the steps when the clerk came out with the results folded in half. Priya took the paper, looked at it a long moment, and held it out without saying anything.

Rose found the notice taped to the circulation desk of the public library, between a flyer for toddler story hour and a laminated map of the county bus routes. First-time volunteers welcome, it said, Saturday, seven a.m., dress for mud. She had been meaning to do something that wasn't school, something that would look less like a line on an application and more like a fact about her, and she had been circumspect about which something, because she distrusted her own motives and didn't want to be the girl who photographed her own kindness. She copied the address onto the back of a receipt and checked out a novel she would not read.

Saturday came cold and clear. The food bank's van waited in the library parking lot, which served as the meeting point, and beside it stood a man in a canvas jacket counting heads on a clipboard. Eleven volunteers, most of them older than Rose, all of them strangers. The man, whose name was Teodoro, drove them out past the edge of town to a farm where the squash field had already been picked over once by the crew that mattered, the paid crew, the main harvest.

"You'll see squash out there still," Teodoro said as they stepped down into the rows. "Anything you gather goes to the food bank. It's called gleaning." He said it the way he might have said the word for a bird or a tool, and then he handed out crates and gloves and walked off toward the far end of the field.

The rows were messy in a way Rose hadn't expected. The plants lay half flattened, and under them the squash had gone pale where the ground had touched them, scarred where a machine had brushed past. She picked one up, turned it over, and hesitated over a soft brown patch the size of her thumb. Whole or not whole. She looked up to ask someone and saw that the other volunteers had already scattered, bent and working, their crates filling without ceremony. Nobody was going to tell her. She set the blemished one aside and kept the rest.

Dana, the volunteer nearest her, was maybe sixty and moved with the ease of a person who had done this many seasons. "Soft spots mean it won't store," Dana said, not looking up. "Hard ones are just ugly. People think food bank means perfect produce, and then it rots in the field because nobody paid for it." Rose asked whether the farmer couldn't sell it, and Dana shrugged one shoulder. "After the main harvest, what's left isn't worth the labor to him. But it's still food. So we come." Rose worked that around while she worked the row. It seemed to her a strange economy, that a thing could be worthless and good at the same time, and she tested the idea against each squash she lifted.

By mid-morning the problem found them. The crates were full, more than half the field still unpicked, and the van had room for only what was crated. The second shift, Teodoro announced from the end of the row, had fallen through, so whatever they didn't get today would be disked into the soil on Monday. Rose watched the volunteers glance at each other, at the sun, at their phones. One by one they began to say they had things, errands, a granddaughter's recital. Teodoro didn't argue. He began stacking crates with the flat efficiency of a man preparing to lose.

Rose had been quiet all morning, and quiet people can sometimes say a thing plainly. "We don't all have to stay," she said. "Some of us could keep picking while the van runs the first load over. Then it comes back for the rest." Dana looked at her, then at the field, then at Teodoro. Teodoro turned his clipboard over as if the answer might be written on the back.

From where Dana stood, it looked like this: a girl of eighteen, mud to the knees of a jacket too thin for the weather, holding a scarred squash in both hands like evidence in a case she was still arguing with herself. Dana had spent enough years in this work to know that schemes hatched at eleven in the morning often died by noon, and she was not going to flatter the girl by pretending otherwise. But she had also spent enough years to know that a full crate driven to the pantry at noon fed someone at six. "I'll stay for the second round," Dana said. "I've got nothing until four." Two of the recital people, cajoled less by Teodoro than by their own shame, muttered that they could stay an hour, and the numbers on the clipboard stopped being a countdown.

The van went loaded and came back empty in time for lunch. Rose's arms ached in a way that felt specific, one muscle for lifting and another for bending, and she had learned that a soft spot was a judgment and an ugly skin was nothing at all. She still wasn't sure, when she thought about the morning, whether she had done a good thing or a merely sensible one, or whether there was a difference, and she decided she would have to come back another Saturday to find out. She stood at the tailgate stacking the last crates, and Dana handed her a squash with a long green scar down its side. "Perfect," Dana said.

Jacob checked the mailbox at 4:15, the way he had every afternoon for nine days, though the mail never came before five. The box was empty except for a coupon circular and a water bill, and he stood there holding the little door open as if another letter might materialize behind the first one. His father had installed the mailbox at the edge of the gravel drive fifteen years ago, sinking the post in concrete, and over time the ground around it had turned friable, so that the whole thing listed toward the road like a man listening for something. Jacob straightened it every so often without thinking. Today he held it upright while he counted the days left before the state university's reply deadline, which was not really a deadline at all, just the last day he could say yes.

The letter, when it came, would be the fourth. Two colleges had already said no, and one had said yes but wanted thirty-eight thousand dollars a year, a figure he had read aloud to his mother and then never mentioned again. The state university was the one he could actually pay for, more or less, which was why his older sister, Dani, had taken over the kitchen table for the past three nights.

He could see her through the window when he came back up the drive, hunched at the laptop with their mother beside her, both of them lit by the screen in the dark kitchen. They were filling out the FAFSA, the form for federal financial aid, and Dani kept explaining it to him in fragments whenever he passed through. "It's how you get the Pell Grant," she said once, not looking up. "Federal money you don't pay back. And federal loans, the ones with the better rates." Another night she added, quieter, "It's not just the federal government. The state uses it too, and the colleges themselves. Almost everybody bases their aid on this one form." Their mother typed the tax numbers with one finger, then two, then asked Dani to read the line back. The state's aid deadline was tomorrow at midnight, and Dani wanted her own answer, a transfer out of the community college and into the nursing program, and that want was tangled up in the same form, the same numbers, the same parents' income.

Jacob had spent the whole application season telling anyone who asked that it was simple math. You ranked the schools, you weighed the costs, you picked the highest expected value. He called it rationalism, half as a joke, when his uncle asked at Christmas how he was choosing. But the math kept refusing to stay simple. The yes for thirty-eight thousand sat in his desk drawer, and every time he opened the drawer for a pencil he felt the weight of it, and he could not make it into a number that behaved. He wanted the big school the way you want a person, which was to say irrationally, and he wanted to be the kind of person who didn't want things that way.

On the ninth night, near eleven, Dani called him into the kitchen. "Read this," she said, and turned the laptop toward him. The form wanted to know whether their parents had filed a joint return, and then it wanted a figure from line something of that return, and their mother had gone to bed with a headache, leaving the question half answered and the deadline two hours off. Jacob found the return in the filing cabinet himself, his hands steady in a way his stomach was not, and read the number while Dani typed it. "So the aid just follows from this?" he asked. "One form, all of it?" "Federal, state, the schools' own money," Dani said. "It all starts here." She hit submit at 11:41 and then sat back and put her hands over her face, and Jacob stood there awkwardly until she said, through her fingers, "Go check the mail. Just in case."

There was nothing, of course. But he stood at the box in the cold anyway, and it was there, with the post leaning against his palm, that he understood something he could not have put in an essay. The form Dani had just filed was a machine for turning one family's circumstances into money, and the machine did not care what he deserved or what he dreamed. That should have made him feel reduced. Instead it felt almost like being absolved. The choice had never been only his; it had been made partly by tax returns and deadlines and whatever Pell Grants added up to, and he could stop treating the wanting as a personal failing.

He came back in and found Dani at the sink, drinking water, the kitchen dark again except the light over the stove. "I decided something," he said. "If the state school takes me, I'm going. The thirty-eight thousand one, I'm letting it go." Dani set down the glass. "Last week you said it was worth the debt if you got in." "Last week I was doing math with feelings and pretending they were numbers," he said. She laughed, a short surprised sound, and then grew serious. "Then maybe I can stop feeling guilty about wanting the nursing program," she said. "Mom keeps saying we can't both." Jacob shrugged. "The form says what it says. We'll see what it says."

The next afternoon he walked down the drive at 4:15 again, knowing better, and stopped anyway when he saw the white edge wedged among the coupons. The envelope was thin, which the internet said could mean anything. He carried it back to the porch steps and sat down with it unopened on his knee, and from inside the house he could hear Dani at the kitchen table, already back on the laptop, looking up the nursing program's aid page. He slid his thumb under the flap and lifted the edge, and the porch boards creaked under him as he leaned forward to read the first line.

The line outside the fire station wound past the hydrant and halfway to the hardware store, and Ella stood in it with her registration card going soft in her hand from the rain. She had forty minutes before her uncle's truck left for the airport, and the line moved in short, stubborn shuffles. Behind her, two volunteers from the Kessler campaign were arguing, not quietly, their clipboards tucked under their arms like shields.

"It's a tie," the taller one said. "Fifty-one to forty-eight, but the margin of error is four points, so it's a tie, and anyone who says otherwise is reading tea leaves."

"It's not a tie," the shorter one said. "Three points is three points."

Eella turned around. "It's within the margin of error," she said, because she had read that phrase in the newspaper on Tuesday and it had lodged in her head like a seed. The taller volunteer looked at her with something between gratitude and suspicion.

The shorter one, whose badge said DARA, shook her head. "It just means the poll can't say who's ahead," Dara said. "Not with confidence. But it doesn't mean they're exactly even." The taller volunteer, MARKUS according to his badge, opened his mouth, closed it, and then said, quietly, "That's not what the guy at the office said."

Eella had spent the drive to the fire station arguing with her own brother about exactly this, and she had lost the argument by being loud rather than right. He had said the poll was a tie; she had said Kessler was winning because the number was bigger; both of them, she understood now, had been claiming more than the number could carry. A poll was not a photograph of the whole town. It was a photograph of a few hundred people, and the margin of error was the smudge on the lens.

"Here's what I can't figure out," Markus said, and now he was talking to her directly, which she regretted and did not regret. "If we can't say Kessler's ahead, then what do we tell people at the doors? The office wants a script by noon. They want us to say the race is tied so nobody stays home."

"Say the poll can't say who's ahead," Ella said. "Say that. It's true and it's shorter than arguing about it."

Dara laughed once, a short bark, and pulled her phone out to check the time. The line moved forward three people. A man in a wet canvas coat near the door was telling anyone who would listen that all polls were lies invented by television stations, and his voice had the bombastic, carrying quality of someone who had decided volume was a form of proof. An older woman in front of Ella turned and said, "Some of us are still voting, Harold," and he subsided.

Eella checked her own phone. Thirty-one minutes. The truck was not going to wait, and her uncle was the kind of man who treated a departure time as a moral test, so missing him would debilitate her whole plan of getting to the airport and, eventually, to the college orientation she was supposed to be flying toward this afternoon. She had built her day like a row of dominoes: vote, truck, plane, new city. The line was the first domino and it refused to fall.

But she was still turning the argument over, because it was the first real thing she had gotten to think about all morning. If the lead was smaller than the margin of error, the poll was silent on the question of who was ahead. It did not say tied. It said nothing, or almost nothing, and there was a difference between nothing and an answer that people kept forgetting. Her brother would say she was splitting hairs. Maybe she was. But the polling place itself was the argument made flesh: five hundred people in a slow line, each one a number no poll had fully counted, each with the ordinary sentience of a person deciding something alone in a booth, which no sample could weigh in advance.

She turned back to the volunteers. "The script could say either candidate could be ahead," she said. "That's what the number actually supports. Then tell people to vote anyway."

Markus wrote it on the back of his flyer, the pen denting the wet paper. "Either candidate could be ahead," he repeated, as if testing whether the words would hold weight. Dara was already dialing the office. The line moved again and Ella was suddenly at the table, showing her card, printing her name in a square, receiving a sticker she pressed onto her jacket without stopping to center it.

In the booth she filled the bubble for Kessler, then stood for a moment with the pen hovering, not over doubt exactly, but over the strangeness of choosing when the numbers had refused to choose for her. She fed the ballot into the machine, heard it click, and walked out into the rain, where the truck was idling at the curb and her uncle was checking his watch.
"Doors close at noon," Markus called after her, waving the flyer. "We'll make it."

She raised a hand without turning around and ran for the passenger door.

Sarah had been at the community center every Tuesday and Thursday since September, first for open gym and then, when the rec league needed a fifth, for the volleyball team that practiced in the echoing gym with the cracked scoreboard. Her father had wanted her to find something structured before college, some discipline to inculcate a routine into her last summer at home, and she had agreed mostly to stop the conversation. Now it was October, and the season was down to three games, and Priya had a doctor's note folded into her sock.

Priya had taken a ball to the temple two weeks earlier, off Sarah's own serve, a shank that nobody could have called. Since then she had come back in stages, and Sarah had learned the shape of it almost without meaning to. First Priya only watched, sitting on the folded mats with the lights dimmed for her. Then she did light jogging along the sideline. Then, last Thursday, she was cleared for the non-contact drills, and tonight she was supposed to try actual play, scrimmaging, the last step before full games.

"Read my note if you want," Priya said, pulling it out of her sock in the hallway by the water fountain. "It says every step, rest to full play, and I only move up if I stay free of symptoms the whole way. One headache and I drop back down." Sarah read it twice. The paper was soft from being carried.

They were eleven minutes into the scrimmage when Sarah noticed Priya standing still at the net, one hand pressed to her eyebrow. Not hurt the way a rolled ankle hurts, but paused, the way you pause in a library. Sarah called the ball early, took the set herself, and put it down flat so the rally ended. Then she walked over.

"Head?"

"Kind of," Priya said. "Started when I tracked Dara's serve. It's not bad."

Coach Reyes blew the whistle and came over, arms crossed, and Sarah watched him weigh it. They needed tonight. Thursday was the semifinal, and Priya was their only real blocker, and everyone on the court knew it. "If it's not bad," he said slowly, "you could sit five and see."

Sarah heard the offer for what it was, and it wasn't dishonest, exactly, but it was specious, a reasonable-sounding cover for wanting her on the floor. She thought of her father, who had argued last week that a promise to yourself was the only contract nobody else could break, and of Priya's note, which said the opposite in a way: that you advanced only when nothing in you objected. For a second the two ideas sat side by side in her head, neither one winning.

"It says while," Sarah said. "You move up only while you're symptom free. Not five minutes of being symptom free." She hadn't planned to say it out loud, and she felt Reyes's eyes on her, but Priya was already nodding, already reaching for her knee pads' strap.

"I know," Priya said. "I go back a stage. Light drills, no scrimmage." She looked at Reyes, and something in her face made the decision hers, which Sarah understood was the only way it could stand. Reyes exhaled through his nose, then shrugged, and told Dara to switch to the net.

After practice Sarah helped Priya carry the ball cart to the equipment closet, because Priya wasn't supposed to lift much yet and because it was a small thing that cost Sarah nothing. They stood in the hallway under the humming fluorescent panel while Priya re-read her own note.

"I'll be honest," Sarah said. "I don't know if the doctor's way is right about everything. Maybe you'd have been fine. Maybe five minutes' rest fixes it and nobody knows." Priya tilted her head, considering, not arguing. "But you're the one who has to live in your head all year," Sarah went on, "and I only have to live with losing Thursday. That math seems pretty easy."

Priya laughed, folded the note, and slid it back into her sock. In the gym, Reyes was killing the lights one bank at a time, and the last square of brightness shrank toward the door where the two of them stood.

"Walk me out," Priya said.

Gabrielle arrived at the farmers' market with her grandmother's canvas bag, forty dollars of her own babysitting money, and a plan she had defended at the kitchen table the night before. Her father wanted spaghetti and meatballs, the same dinner they had eaten every Sunday since she could remember, a tradition she privately considered parochial, as though the family palate had stopped exploring somewhere around 1998. She wanted to cook the pork loin from the Hsu farm stand, with the plums and the rosemary, the recipe she had torn from a magazine and taped inside her notebook like a confession. In the end she bought both, because in her family refusing anyone anything was a kind of arson.

She moved through the stalls with purpose, joking with Mr. Alvarez about whether his tomatoes were as good as he claimed, and letting him eviscerate a competitor's melons with one raised eyebrow. She counted her change. She argued herself down from the flowers and then, at the last stall, argued herself back up. By eleven she was carrying pork, plums, rosemary, a bag of tomatoes "for the meatballs, in case," and a terrible confidence that dinner would prove something, though she could not have said what.

Her brother Theo had left for college in August, and he texted while she was waiting in line for bread. "Cooking the family meal? Who are you and what have you done with my sister." Then, a second message: "Seriously though. Dad will say it's too fancy. Mom will say it's delicious to spite him. Report back." She read it twice, smiling, and did not answer yet, because answers felt like promises.

She cooked in the late afternoon with the kitchen windows open, the plums collapsing into the pan, the pork seared and then resting under foil. Her mother drifted through and stole a plum. Her father drifted through and said, "Smells like a restaurant," which in his dialect could mean anything. He changed his mind before dinner, though, out loud, at the table, which for him was practically opera. "This," he said, pointing his fork at the plums, "is better than the meatballs. Don't tell the meatballs." Everyone laughed, even Gabrielle, even the dog, who was hoping to be consulted.

Afterward they sat on the back porch in the blue evening, and it was hot, the kind of hot where the porch swing complained and the lemonade went watery. The platters came out with them, because no one wanted to go back inside, and the pork sat in its juices on the table while they argued about whether Aunt Rosa's new boyfriend was truly terrible or just boring, a debate with a long and distinguished history. Gabrielle looked at the meat and felt a small cold thought arrive.

She went inside and found the thermometer magnet on the fridge, the one from a food safety pamphlet her mother had never read. Her phone was faster. She searched, and there it was, plain as arithmetic: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or for more than one hour when it's above 90. She read it twice. She stepped back onto the porch, where the air itself felt like a held breath, thick and ninety-something, and looked at the clock inside her own head. They had been out here longer than one hour. Longer than two.

"Everything's done," she said, gathering the platters, and her father said, "Done?" and she said, "Done for. The meat. It's been sitting out in this heat, and the rule is two hours in the danger zone, one hour if it's over ninety, and we are way past one." Her mother said, "The danger zone," slowly, as though tasting the phrase. "That sounds like a movie your brother would like." Gabrielle scraped the pork and the plums into the trash while her father mourned quietly and dramatically, one hand on his chest, and the dog watched the garbage can with frank theological despair.

Later, alone in the kitchen, she washed the pan and thought about her grandmother, who had raised five kids on leftovers and prayer and would have laughed at the waste, and about Theo's food science textbooks, which he quoted at dinner like scripture. Two inheritances, and she could hold both, she decided, roughly; she would trust the thermometer and the rule, and she would cook less next time, and she would still not tell her grandmother. The plums had been perfect, though, and the pork was gone, and there was no version of tonight without that.

She texted Theo a photo of the empty trash can and the thermometer magnet. "You were right about the danger zone. Dad loved dinner and then I eviscerated it, per USDA. Consanguinity entitles you to half the blame for my cooking genes." She dried her hands and set the pan back on the stove, and outside, faintly, she could hear her father and the dog, negotiating over the last piece of bread.

Jackson had been volunteering at the Harbor Street Community Office for six weeks, and until Tuesday morning nobody had asked him to write anything.

Mrs. Adeyemi, the coordinator, called him over to the desk by the window. "I need a favor," she said. "Dara's out sick, and this email to the parks department has to go out by noon. The grant meeting is Thursday, and if we don't confirm the picnic shelter by then, we lose it." She slid a printout across the desk. "Read this and tell me what you think."

Jackson read it. Dara, the part-time staffer, had written a page and a half about the history of the summer program, the weather last July, a complaint about a broken water fountain, and then, in the final paragraph, a request to reserve the Riverside shelter on August 12. It meandered like a river deciding where to go. He could tell Dara was trying to sound professional, stacking formal phrases to burnish the message, but the polish hid the point instead of brightening it.

"It's polite," he said carefully. "It's just that the ask is buried."

"Can you fix it by eleven?" Mrs. Adeyemi was already halfway back to the phone, where a parent was asking about bus passes. "Keep it respectful. Mr. Okafor over there can be touchy about tone, so don't be blunt."

Jackson sat down at the volunteer computer. He typed a draft, deleted it, typed another. The question he kept circling was simple and stubborn: what did a professional voice actually sound like? He'd written school essays meant to impress a teacher, but this was different. Somebody on the other end had forty other emails and a shelter calendar, and the kindest thing might be to stop performing and just say the thing.

He was still rearranging paragraphs when Ren, the college intern, leaned over his shoulder with a granola bar. "What's the mess?"

"Trying to figure out where the request goes," Jackson said. "Dara put it last, like a reveal."

Ren chewed for a second. "My cousin's in the Navy. She drills this into everybody. 'Bottom Line Up Front', BLUF. It's a US military writing standard. You put the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details."

"So the ask goes first, and the reasons come after."

"Exactly. She says nobody overseas has time to hunt for the point."

Jackson turned back to the screen. It felt almost rude, like walking into someone's office and talking before saying hello. But maybe, he thought, leading with the request was a form of respect, an admission that the reader's time mattered. He wrote a new draft.

Dear Mr. Okafor,

I'm writing to confirm our reservation of the Riverside picnic shelter for August 12, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., for the Harbor Street summer program's family day, roughly 80 attendees.

If the shelter is available, could you reply by Wednesday so we can finalize the grant paperwork? Below is the background, in case it's useful.

He kept the history Dara had gathered but cut it to four sentences. He left out the water fountain complaint entirely, then second-guessed himself and added one line, since Dara had clearly wanted it mentioned: "Separately, we'd appreciate knowing when the drinking fountain near the east entrance might be repaired." Maybe that was wrong, mixing requests. Maybe it was honest. He couldn't decide, and he let it stand.

Mrs. Adeyemi read it at 11:20, her face dour with deadline worry until the second line, when it eased. "This is good. Short and clear." Then she paused. "The fountain thing. He'll read that as a criticism of his department."

"Is that bad? Dara wanted it on record."

"It's a question of whether we need the shelter more than we need the complaint." She handed it back. "Your call. You're the one writing it."

Jackson sat with it for a moment. Two instincts pulled at him: Dara's instinct to document everything, soften everything, wrap the point in velvet; and the BLUF instinct to state the point and get out of the way. Neither felt complete on its own. The email could be direct and still be generous. He moved the fountain line to the end, after the background, and reworded it: "One small unrelated note, no urgency: the drinking fountain near the east entrance has been out of service, and families would be glad when it's working again."

He hit send at 11:52.

At 2:40 the reply came. Mr. Okafor confirmed the shelter, said he'd have the permit signed by Wednesday morning, and added a single line about the fountain: a work order had been filed in June, and he would check on its status. Then, at the bottom: "Thank you for making your request easy to find."

Mrs. Adeyemi printed it and pinned it to the corkboard above the office printer. "Dara should see this when she's back," she said, and Jackson noticed she'd circled the last sentence in red pen.

He stood there a minute longer than he needed to, reading it again. He still didn't know whether he'd been right to keep the fountain line at all, or whether softening it had been wisdom or cowardice. That part stayed unresolved, the way real things did. But he copied the email into a file he labeled "forms and templates," and saved it under a new folder name: BLUF, and other things I don't know yet.

Ren passed by with the last of the granola bar. "So what's the verdict? Military style?"

"Half," Jackson said. "Blunt up front, polite at the back."

"Sounds like stoicism with manners," Ren said, and laughed.

Jackson didn't answer, but he wrote that down too.

The argument John had prepared was about heredity and choice. He had written it on two sides of an index card the night before: that a person's observable traits, the phenotype, set certain conditions, but that conditions were not commands, and that anyone who claimed genes dictated a life had skipped a step. He wanted to say it well. He had been quiet in this class since September, and Mr. Okafor had asked him twice, gently, whether he had thoughts he was saving for later. Today he had a card with him, and a raised hand, and the small honest want of a boy who wanted to be heard getting it right.

The discussion had already started when the bell stopped ringing. Marcus was talking, leaning back with his chair on two legs, about a magazine article claiming that scientists had proved people were born criminals. "So if your genes say you're going to steal," Marcus said, "punishment is basically pointless. That's the logical conclusion of the whole genetic position." A few people nodded. Someone near the window said, grimly, that he refused to believe humans were just meat programs.

John put his hand up and made his argument, reading partly from the card and partly from somewhere braver. He said the phenotype was a starting condition, like the terrain a road is built on, and that roads went many ways across the same terrain. He said the evidence for influence was not evidence for fate. When he finished, the room was quiet in a way he could not read, and then Marcus dropped his chair forward with a bang.

"So you're saying it doesn't matter how kids are raised," Marcus said. "If it's all in the genes anyway, then bad parents are off the hook, and we can just malign poor families for their DNA and call it science. That's what you're defending." He spread his hands, as though the conclusion were obvious and a little dirty. Around him, people were frowning, but the frowns were aimed at John now, at the ugly thing Marcus had placed in his mouth, something about eugenics and excuses, a position John had never taken and would never take.

"That's not what I said," John managed. His voice came out thinner than he wanted. "I said influence, not control." But Marcus was already talking over him, generously offering to agree to disagree, as if he had done John a favor by dismantling him. John looked down at his index card, at his own tidy handwriting, and felt the strange vertigo of being defeated by an argument that had never touched his own.

Across the room, Dana had stopped doodling. She had written down both claims in her notebook, in her cramped shorthand, one under the other: John's actual words, and Marcus's reply. The two did not match. Marcus had not answered the road built across terrain; he had answered something easier, a flimsier version standing where John had been standing, and he was swinging at it as though it were the same thing. She raised her hand, and when Mr. Okafor nodded to her, she turned toward Marcus rather than the teacher.

"That's a straw man," she said. "You attacked a weaker, distorted version of his argument instead of the argument he actually made, and you're acting like the two are the same." Marcus opened his mouth, and Dana pointed at her notebook, which was not a normal thing to do, and read John's sentence back verbatim, then read Marcus's rebuttal verbatim. "He said influence, not control," she said. "You answered control. If it's a fallacy, the whole reply just falls off the argument, like knocking over a dummy and claiming you beat the man." The class was very still. Marcus said, "Fine, then he should have been clearer," which was not the same as conceding, and everyone seemed to know it.

Mr. Okafor asked whether John wanted to respond, and John found that the moment had changed shape on him. He had planned for opposition, for a real counterargument about twin studies or free will, and what he had gotten instead was a distortion, which required a different move: not to defend his claim harder, but to first restore it, to say, "Before you argue with me, argue with me." He said that, almost exactly, and heard a couple of people laugh quietly, the good kind of laugh. Then he said the part he was less sure of, because it was true. "I don't actually know where influence ends," he said. "I know it's not everything. I can't tell you the percentage, and I don't think anyone in this room can. If you want to beat my real argument, that's the place to hit it, because that's where I'm standing."

Marcus looked at him for a long second, chair flat on the floor now, and then said, "All right. Say more about the percentage thing." John put the index card face down on his desk, because he was about to go off it, and started talking.

Landon found the cap first, then the gown, then the tassel, in that order, in three different places: the cap under his bed, the gown on the laundry hook where it had been since March, the tassel in a mug on his desk that said WORLD'S OKAYEST FISHERMAN, a gift from an uncle who had never seen him fish. The ceremony was in nine hours. His mother was already in the kitchen making potato salad for the party, halving eggs with a serrated knife, which he had told her a hundred times was wrong and which she did anyway.

The problem was the speech. Two weeks earlier, when Mr. Ruiz had asked him to speak for the class, Landon had said yes because it was easier than saying no, and now he had a legal pad with four false starts on it and a fifth one that ended mid-sentence at the word "meanwhile." He had tried solemn. He had tried funny. Both had desiccated on the page, the jokes curling up like the edges of the eggs his mother was currently butchering. He sat at the kitchen table with the pad while she worked, and she did not ask about the speech, because she knew him well enough not to.

The party started at two, in the backyard, under a canopy his stepfather had borrowed from a man at work. People came in a slow tide: aunts, neighbors, kids Landon had known since trundle beds, kids he had met in eleventh grade and liked fine. Dana Okafor arrived with her grandmother and a casserole and the expression of someone surveying a land she had once ruled. Gus came late, as Gus did, carrying a basketball even though there was no game planned.

It was Gus, actually, standing at the drink table with a red cup, who said it. "Where's Ricky Solano? And those O'Malley twins. I figured they'd be here even if they didn't walk." He counted on his fingers, half joking, and then stopped counting because the list got longer than a joke could carry. "We started with like 340."

"There's, what, 290 walking tomorrow," Dana said. She had a way of saying numbers like she was handing you change. Landon watched her do the arithmetic in her head and then pull out her phone, because even Dana checked. She scrolled, frowned, scrolled again, and turned the screen toward them. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." She said it flat, like reading a train schedule. "That's the whole country, that year."

"So we're average," Gus said.

"We're a data point," said Dana, and put the phone away, and took a cupcake.

Landon had been drifting toward his own speech problem all afternoon, the way a loose tooth finds the tongue, and now he could not stop pressing on it. He walked to the far end of the yard, past the canopy, where the grass turned to dirt near the fence, and stood there doing what he always did with numbers: turning them into faces. Ricky Solano, who had moved junior year and sent one Snap after that. The O'Malley twins. A girl named Priya who had left mid-October of sophomore year without a word, whose locker he had watched get taped over and reassigned. Thirteen percent of somewhere. But that was the country, that year, not his class, and his class was not a fixed thing either, kids arriving and leaving like weather. He understood the statistic and did not understand his class, and he understood his class, in the face-by-face way, and could not fit it to the statistic, and both of those were true, and he stood in the dirt trying to hold them at once.

His mother found him there. "You're hiding," she said.

"I'm drafting."

"In the dirt."

"Where no one can see me delete things."

She looked at him for a moment, and there was a kind of clemency in it, the look she gave when she had decided not to say the thing she plainly wanted to say, which was that he could still call Mr. Ruiz and back out. "Potato salad's out," she said instead. "It has eggs in it. That's all I'll say."

Later, when the canopy lights came on and the yard shrank into its own small bright country, Gus stole the mic from the borrowed speaker, supposedly to lead a toast, mostly to stall for Landon. "Our valedictorian," Gus announced, mispronouncing it deliberately, "is still writing." A laugh moved through the tectonic shift of folding chairs, everyone turning toward Landon at the same geological speed.

He stood up. He did not have the legal pad. He had a sentence he had built walking back across the grass, and he knew only the first half of it. "Some of the people we started with aren't here," he said, "and some of them we could have called and didn't, and the numbers say that's ordinary, and I can't tell yet whether ordinary makes it better or worse." He stopped there. It was not an ending. Dana raised her red cup without a word, and after a second, everyone else did too, and Gus whispered, "Nine a.m., you're on," and turned the music back up.

Mya found her father in the kitchen at six in the morning, standing before the cleared end of the counter with a shoebox of photographs and no idea what to do with it. The funeral had been in March, which meant her grandmother had been gone long enough that the grief had changed shape, become quieter and more portable, and now here was November arriving with its own demands. On the counter her father had already set a jar of marigolds he must have bought on his way home from the night shift, the orange almost too loud against the white tile.

"She liked the pan de muerto from the bakery on Cesar Chavez," he said, not turning around. "The one with the sesame seeds, not the sugar."

Mya hadn't known that. She knew her grandmother's coffee, black with too much sugar, and the way she could be bellicose about politics at the dinner table, going after uncles twice her size until somebody changed the subject to soccer. But the sweet bread, the specific bakery, the sesame versus the sugar, all of that belonged to her father's childhood, not to hers. He had grown up in this city with the grandmother; Mya had grown up three states away, visiting in summers, receiving birthday cards with five-dollar bills folded inside.

"Is this an altar?" she asked. "Like a real one?"

"An ofrenda," he said. "We build them November first and second. Day of the Dead. Photos, her favorite foods, her drinks. Whatever she loved."

He said it plainly, the way he said everything, and she understood he was not performing a tradition so much as returning to one, the way you return to a house you lived in as a child and find the light switches with your hands in the dark. Mya had been raised half in that house and half outside it. Her mother was from Ohio and had never vilified the old customs, exactly, but had a way of calling them "your father's side of things" that kept them at a certain distance, and Mya had let that distance stand because it was easier than learning what was on the other side of it.

She took the shoebox from the counter and sat at the table to go through it. The photos were curled and some had lost their corners. Her grandmother at thirty, squinting into sun. Her grandmother at the stove in this same kitchen, younger than Mya was now, holding a cast-iron pan. Her grandmother holding a baby who had to be her father. Mya tried to match the kitchen in the photograph to the kitchen around her, the window, the doorframe, and felt something she could only call synchronicity, two moments occupying the same few square feet of tile, forty years apart, herself the only witness to both.

"I should have come more," she said. "Last summer especially. She asked me to come help her can the tomatoes and I said I had a program."

Her father was quiet while he folded a cloth, cream-colored with embroidered edges, and laid it over a stack of boxes that had been in the garage. The cloth had to be older than either of them. "She knew you had a program," he said finally. "She told everybody at church her granddaughter had a program. She wasn't confused about it."

"But she asked anyway."

"She asked anyway." He set a framed photo on the cloth and studied it. "People ask anyway. That's mostly what asking is."

The bakery opened at seven. Mya drove because her father's eyes were tired from the shift, and she stood in line behind a woman buying four loaves and a tray of sugar skulls wrapped in cellophane. The bread was still warm when the baker handed it over, dusted with sesame, round with the little knobs of dough on top. In the car she held the bag on her lap and her father didn't say anything, and she thought about how a person could keep existing in bread, in a folded cloth, in the specific absence of sugar on a crust, long after the funeral, and how she still couldn't decide whether that was comfort or just the shape a missing person leaves.

Back in the kitchen she set the loaf on the cloth beside the coffee cup, the good one with the gold rim, filled with black coffee and too much sugar. Her father placed the photograph of the grandmother at the stove, and Mya added the one of the baby, and they stepped back at the same moment. Then her father went to answer his phone in the other room, and Mya stood alone in front of the ofrenda with the marigolds and the bread and the two photographs, and she said, out loud, "I'll come next summer. I'll help with the tomatoes." She reached forward and turned the coffee cup a quarter turn, so the gold rim faced the window and the morning light caught it.

The gallery was cold in the way of rooms that guard their canvases more carefully than their visitors, and Marcus stood in front of a painting of nested squares with his sketchbook clamped under one arm. He had come because Ms. Rothenberg had said his portfolio application needed a theme, ten pieces that spoke to each other, and he had said "fine" in the tone he used when he meant the opposite. Now he wrote in his sketchbook, "squares? boring?" and crossed it out.

"You've been standing there for ten minutes," said Priya, appearing beside him with her coat still on. They had applied to the same summer intensive, and though they had never quite called themselves friends, they had fallen into the habit of being honest with each other because it was easier than performing.

"Ten minutes," Marcus said. "Ten pieces. I keep counting."

Priya leaned in and read the wall label. "Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976. Keeping the nested squares constant while changing only the colours." She said it flatly, like reading a bus schedule, and then looked at him. "A thousand. For twenty-six years. Same squares."

"That's the part I can't get past." Marcus turned his sketchbook toward her so she could see the page, which held, instead of drawings, a list of themes he had considered and abandoned: doors, his grandmother's hands, the river by the train tracks, each one crossed out with a different weight of pen. "I keep thinking a theme means finding something profound. He just picked a shape and stayed."

"Maybe staying is the profound part."

He didn't answer, because a docent was shepherding a cluster of middle-schoolers past them, and one of the kids said, loudly, that anyone could paint squares, and the docent laughed in a way that agreed. Marcus felt an old defensiveness rise, the same one he'd felt two years ago in Mr. Ito's studio class when a boy named Devon had called Marcus's color studies "easy" and Marcus had thrown away three weeks of work rather than let them be maligned. He had regretted that for a long time, though he had never said so to anyone. The torn canvases had gone out with the recycling on a Tuesday, and he had watched the truck take them, and had told himself it was about standards.

Outside the museum, the January light was the flat white of an unwritten page. Priya unwrapped a granola bar and split it without being asked, which was how she apologized for things she wouldn't name. "So say you did it," she said. "Same composition, ten times, one thing different each time. What's your one thing?"

"Colour," Marcus said, and then heard himself and laughed. "Which is just doing Albers again."

"Doing Albers again is also over a thousand pieces deep. You'd be doing it once." She chewed and looked at the traffic on Bloor Street. "It's a truism that you have to find your own voice, but nobody says the voice might start as someone else's mouth moving."

He wrote that down, because it was better than anything on his list. "My grandmother's kitchen," he said slowly. "It's yellow. It's been yellow my whole life. Except it hasn't, not really, it's been six different yellows, and I only noticed when my uncle painted it that grey-blue last spring and she hated it so much she cried." He was talking faster now, his cold breath visible. "Same kitchen. Same window over the sink, same table. Only the colour changing, and it changed whether the whole room felt like hers."

Priya stopped chewing. "That's not squares."

"No. But it's the method." He flipped to a clean page and drew a quick rectangle, the kitchen, and nested inside it the window, and inside the window whatever was outside. He drew it four times, small, and wrote above each one a different word: mustard, cream, the grey-blue, and one he left blank. "It's parsimonious," he said, half apologizing, "but maybe that's not bad. One decision, repeated, and every difference means something because the composition isn't fighting for attention."

"That word sounds like an insult."

"It's the opposite." He looked at the four rectangles, then across the street at a building whose windows were reflecting a colour of sky he couldn't name, and realized he was already mixing it in his head, and that the blank word would have to stay blank for now, because he did not yet know what his grandmother's kitchen would become, or whether she would ever forgive the grey-blue, or whether ten pieces could hold a thing he understood only as a feeling in a room. "I'm going to need her to send me photographs," he said. "Before and after."

The gym smelled like rubber and cold air, and Florence had the ball at the top of the key with eleven seconds left in a scrimmage nobody was supposed to care about. She cared. She had missed her last four shots, every one rattling off the back rim, and now Coach Voss was yelling from the sideline, "Swing it, Flo, swing it," because everyone on the floor believed the same thing: a girl who has missed four in a row will miss the fifth.

She swung it.
